articles.title: Elena Rybakina rallies to beat Coco Gauff, book US Open final
articles.summary: NEW YORK–Elena Rybakina rallied from a set down to beat Coco Gauff 3-6, 6-4, 6-4 on Thursday and book a US Open championship showdown with two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka. In…

blocks.text: Elena Rybakina, of Kazakhstan, reacts as she wins her match against Coco Gauff, of the United States, during the women’s singles semifinals of the U.S. Open tennis championships Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Frank Franklin II)
NEW YORK–Elena Rybakina rallied from a set down to beat Coco Gauff 3-6, 6-4, 6-4 on Thursday and book a US Open championship showdown with two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka.
In Saturday’s final Rybakina will try to deal another blow to Sabalenka, having knocked her out of the number one world ranking just by reaching the semi-finals.
“I feel like I definitely need to step my game up, serve much better than today and stay aggressive,” Rybakina said of her looming clash with Sabalenka.

Gauff’s bid to return to the final for the first time since she defeated Sabalenka for the 2023 title had got off to a smooth start, with the American seizing the initiative in the opening set with a break to go 4-2 up.

blocks.caption: Coco Gauff, of the United States, left, greets Elena Rybakina, of Kazakhstan, after Rybakina won their match during the women's singles semifinals of the U.S. Open tennis championships Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, in New York. (

blocks.text: Coco Gauff, of the United States, left, greets Elena Rybakina, of Kazakhstan, after Rybakina won their match during the women’s singles semifinals of the U.S. Open tennis championships Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth)
She held to love to take a 5-2 lead and then held in the ninth game to take a one set lead.
But Rybakina hit back with an early break of serve in the second set for a 3-1 lead and held to go 4-1 up.
Gauff responded superbly to claw her way back into contention with a break to make it 4-3 before holding to square it a 4-4.
Yet she was unable to make the most of her fightback and double-faulted in the 10th game to hand two set points to Rybakina at 15-40. Rybakina pounced on that chance to take the match to a third set.
The decisive set followed a similar pattern.
Gauff conceded a break to trail 5-3 and leave Rybakina serving for the match.
But the American broke back immediately to make it 5-4 to get it back on serve.
Again though Gauff was unable to capitalize, and a deft volley from Rybakina left her with two match points at 15-40, before Gauff then hit a wide open smash long to hand her opponent victory.
“It was such a cool third set — I feel like I was a little bit lucky on her serve,” Rybakina said. “A couple of deep returns, one mistake from her, it went quickly my way…it was a real battle.”

articles.title: Lawyer Edgar Gica faces probe over alleged drunk driving, hit-and-run
articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines — The Land Transportation Office Region VII (LTO-7) is currently investigating an allegation that Attorney Edgar Gica was driving drunk when the Mercedes-Benz allegedly struck…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines — The Land Transportation Office Region VII (LTO-7) is currently investigating an allegation that Attorney Edgar Gica was driving drunk when the Mercedes-Benz allegedly struck multiple vehicles before crashing into a bakery in Cebu City.

Gica, father of Dumanjug Mayor Efren “Gungun” Gica, was identified as the driver of the vehicle involved in the September 9 incident along V. Rama Avenue, according to a traffic incident report and an LTO-7 Show Cause Order.
In a statement issued Friday, September 11, LTO-7 said the alleged drunk driving is among the circumstances being examined in the administrative investigation.

The agency is also looking into whether the reported incidents violated existing land transportation laws, including reckless or imprudent operation of a motor vehicle, the duties of a driver involved in a vehicular accident, and provisions under Republic Act No. 10586, or the Anti-Drunk and Drugged Driving Act of 2013.
Allegedly struck several vehicles

The LTO-7 show-cause order said the administrative investigation stemmed from widespread media coverage of a hit-and-run incident involving a gray Mercedes-Benz sedan, reportedly driven by Gica, at around 11 p.m. on September 9 along V. Rama Avenue.

Based on initial information received by the agency, the vehicle allegedly struck several motorcycles before proceeding toward Barangay San Nicolas, Cebu City, where it subsequently crashed into a bakery.
Law enforcement authorities attempted to stop the vehicle following the incident. However, Gica failed or refused to pull over and instead continued driving toward San Nicolas.
The LTO said the alleged collisions, failure to stop when signaled by authorities, and continued operation of the vehicle until it crashed into the bakery warranted an administrative investigation.
Police report

A traffic incident report from the Cebu City Police Office’s Traffic Enforcement Unit (TEU) said Gica was being escorted for further investigation following an earlier collision with a taxi along Tormis Street, Sambag 1, when he struck a parked Honda Beat motorcycle and an e-bike near Shell V. Rama Gas Station.
Gica sustained injuries from the crash and was brought to Miller Hospital, while the Mercedes-Benz was impounded and taken to the TEU office.
The report said Gica, through his son Efren Z. Gica, settled the incident on site with the owners of the bakeshop, motorcycle, and e-bike.
The 63-year-old taxi driver later went to the TEU office and identified the Mercedes-Benz as the vehicle that hit his taxi, which sustained a scratch on its rear left-side passenger door.
Another vehicle owner also reported that his Honda Civic had been sideswiped by the older Gica’s vehicle.
Both the taxi driver and the vehicle owner expressed their intention not to pursue criminal negligence charges, provided Gica shoulders their vehicle repair expenses.
Administrative investigation vs Edgar Gica
Gica was directed to appear before the LTO-7 Operations Division and submit his written comment or explanation, together with pertinent documents and evidence.
Pending the investigation, LTO-7 has preventively suspended his driver’s license and placed the Mercedes-Benz under alarm.

articles.title: Sandigan justice rebuffs 4-6 week recovery plan for Romualdez: Minumura na kami ng tao
articles.summary: Sandiganbayan Associate Justice Ronald Moreno scored Thursday the four to six weeks recovery plan for Leyte Representative and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 1:50pm
Sandiganbayan Associate Justice Ronald Moreno scored Thursday the four to six weeks recovery plan for Leyte Representative and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
“Minumura na kami ng tao rito (The public has been cursing us here),” Moreno said during Day 2 of the hearing on Romualdez’s motion for hospital detention.
Dr. Rody Sy, the lawmaker's cardiologist, said Romualdez would need four to six weeks to recover from his ailments due to stress
He said Romualdez’s blood pressure reached as much as 170/110 on Thursday, prompting his doctors to adjust the level of medicines given to him.
He said the medicine for controlling blood pressure was given two hours earlier at 6 pm, while the medicine to address sleep deprivation was adjusted from half a tablet to one tablet.

“He can be transferred to another facility with the same capacity, but at this time, it might not be appropriate. I feel his [medical] condition has to be controlled first before allowing him to be transferred,” Sy said.
“It would take him four to six weeks to recover from his stress factors. It (transfer) would not be ideal, knowing what is going on. He is under extreme stress,” he added.

Sy conceded that the pending criminal case and his warrant of arrest were included in the factors as to why the lawmaker was suffering from extreme stress, among other ailments such as hypertension and diabetes.
“I think it is a big factor,” he said.
Sy, however, said that Romualdez can be transferred to another facility for examination by government doctors.
“Puwede naman (That can be done),” he said. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: What to know about BARMM’s first parliamentary elections
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — After four postponements, the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will finally be held on Sept. 14. Here are the key…

blocks.text: What to know about BARMM’s first parliamentary elections
MANILA, Philippines — After four postponements, the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will finally be held on Sept. 14.
Here are the key things to know about the elections:
The BARMM parliamentary elections
The elections will determine the members of the Bangsamoro Parliament, the legislative body of the BARMM established under the Bangsamoro Organic Law, or Republic Act (RA) No. 11054.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said last month that the elections are crucial to the development of the region, which he described as a product of a decadeslong peace process that began in 1968.

Marcos said the participation of former secessionists in the elections, including through campaigning, shows that they have chosen the political process over armed struggle to pursue peace and progress in the region.
Why were the elections postponed?

RA No. 11054, which established the BARMM in 2019, initially scheduled the first parliamentary elections for May 2022, when the mandate of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) was expected to end.
The elections were later moved to May 2025, then to Oct. 13 of the same year under RA No. 12123.
RA No. 12317 eventually reset the elections to the second Monday of September, which falls on Sept. 14 this year.
RELATED STORY: Zubiri launches book on Bangsamoro Organic Law creation

Sen. Juan Miguel Zubiri, the principal author of the law that created the BARMM, earlier said the latest postponement was necessary to give the region more time for institution-building, address governance limitations and ensure a smoother transition.
Seats at stake
Under the Bangsamoro Organic Law, signed by then-President Rodrigo Duterte, voters will elect 80 members of Parliament:

items: 40 party representatives
32 district representatives
Eight sectoral representatives

blocks.text: The sectoral seats are reserved for women, youth, traditional leaders, ulama or Islamic scholars, settler communities and other sectors.
Who can voters choose?
The parliamentary system is designed to provide voters with different forms of representation, according to the BTA.
On election day, voters will make eight choices: one regional political party, one district representative and six sectoral representatives.
For the regional parliamentary political party, voters will choose a party rather than an individual candidate.
The 40 regional party-representative seats will be distributed based on each party’s share of the vote, with the party’s nominees filling the seats it wins.
For the parliamentary district representative, voters will choose one individual candidate to represent their parliamentary district.
“Because the Bangsamoro has 32 district seats, the candidates on the ballot will depend on the voter’s registered district,” the BTA said.
For the sectoral representatives, voters will choose two representatives for settler communities and one each for women, youth, traditional leaders and ulama.
More than 2 million voters
Based on data from the Commission on Elections (Comelec), 2.393 million voters are registered for the BARMM elections.
They will cast their votes through 5,212 clustered precincts in 1,186 voting centers across the region.
In January, the BTA passed Parliament Bill No. 415, a measure providing for the apportionment of parliamentary district representative seats in the BARMM.
The measure established the region’s 32 parliamentary districts, clearing the final legal requirement for the elections to proceed.
Last year, the BTA failed to pass the redistricting bill despite an earlier commitment to do so by Dec. 31.
The measure was needed to comply with a Supreme Court decision that, without an approved districting framework, the Comelec could not proceed with election preparations.
Parliament Bill No. 415 was approved on third and final reading before dawn on Jan. 13 following a special session that began Jan. 12. It received 48 votes in favor, 19 against and four abstentions.
The recent postponement
Two weeks after the BTA approved the districting measure, the Comelec postponed the March 30, 2026, Bangsamoro Parliamentary Election.
“Legally and operationally, we can no longer hold the BPE on March 30,” Comelec Chairman George Garcia said. “Operationally, we can no longer afford the one month and two weeks to hold the BPE.”
Marcos eventually signed into law the bill resetting the first regular elections in the BARMM to the second Monday of September.

The Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity commended the BTA for passing the new districting law, calling it a major step toward holding the region’s first regular parliamentary elections.

“The passage of Parliament Bill No. 415 in a special session on January 12 is seen as a major step by the BTA towards establishing a fully functioning, representative, and democratic government in the Bangsamoro, anchored on the provisions of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB),” it said.

Then-Presidential Peace Adviser Carlito G. Galvez Jr. said the approval of a legally compliant redistricting law reflected the BTA’s resolve to uphold democratic principles, ensure inclusive representation and realize the aspirations of Bangsamoro communities for self-governance.

“The law’s passage aligns with the peace, reconciliation and unity agenda of the Marcos administration, and its commitment to uphold its deliverables under all signed Bangsamoro peace agreements,” he said.
Government never lost hope

Despite the postponements, Marcos said that “the government never lost hope and remains fully committed to supporting this democratic exercise,” adding that “we are prepared for the first parliamentary elections in the BARMM.”
He made the statement during the opening ceremony of the 2026 National Peace Consciousness Month at the Ceremonial Hall of Malacañan Palace.

The monthlong observance commemorates the 30th anniversary of the signing of the 1996 Final Peace Agreement with the Moro National Liberation Front, the 40th anniversary of the 1986 Mount Data Peace Accord and the signing of the Agreement on the Fulfillment of the Mount Data Peace Accord with the Cordillera Bodong Administration-Cordillera People’s Liberation Army.

“Be assured that this Administration will do everything within our mandate to ensure that the elections are safe, peaceful, and credible. We will protect the right of every Bangsamoro voter to cast a ballot freely and without fear,” Marcos said.
He urged BARMM voters to show that the region’s future is shaped by their voices, choices and hopes for their communities.
Officials elected in the BARMM parliamentary elections will serve from noon Oct. 30, 2026, to June 30, 2031.
Beginning in 2031, elected officials will assume office at noon June 30 following their election.

RA No. 12317 states that, to synchronize the BARMM parliamentary elections with the national and local polls, regular elections for the Bangsamoro Government will be held on the second Monday of May 2031 and every three years thereafter. /dm — with reports from Luisa Cabato

articles.title: Sara Duterte calls out 'political harassment' after Madriaga case junked
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte accused the administration of political harassment after the perjury complaint she filed against her alleged former bagman Ramil Madriaga has been dismissed.

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 1:41pm
Vice President Sara Duterte accused the administration of political harassment after the perjury complaint she filed against her alleged former bagman Ramil Madriaga was dismissed.

“Well, makikita natin yung pattern na kapag nagsisinungaling yung isang tao, nagsisinungaling yung isang kidnapper ay okay lang. Basta sa nakakatulong yun sa political harassment ng administrasyon,” she said in an ambush interview.
(Well, we can see the pattern that when a person lies, a kidnapper lies, it's okay. As long as it helps the political harassment of the administration.)
The Office of the City Prosecutor of Taguig earlier dismissed the perjury complaint filed by Duterte against Madriaga for “lack of prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty to conviction.”
Madriaga, who identified himself as a former aide of Duterte, alleged that drug dealers and Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGO) operators were funding a campaign for the Vice President.

In her perjury complaint, Duterte said that Madriaga’s accusations were disproven by certifications from the Presidential Security Command, Office of the Vice President, Davao City Government, among others.
She also claimed that Madriaga crafted his statements from publicly available information.
Asked about calls for her disbarment over her statement of lack of trust with the courts, Duterte expressed openness for the possible complaints.
“We will take each case as they come and we will answer each complaint as they come,” she said.
Malacañang earlier said the Supreme Court could investigate Duterte’s recent remarks that she does not trust the Philippine courts.

Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro was asked whether Duterte’s statements could constitute conduct unbecoming of a member of the Bar and potentially serve as a basis for disciplinary action or disbarment.

“Siguro po ang Supreme Court na po natin ang makakasagot niyan. Maaari naman po ang Supreme Court na magsagawa ng motu proprio or on its own initiative na pag-iimbestiga patungkol po dito,” Castro said.
(Maybe our Supreme Court can answer that. The Supreme Court can conduct a motu proprio, or on its own initiative, investigation into this.) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Kim Chiu’s sister Lakam charged over alleged P44-million theft
articles.summary: Lakam Chiu, the older sister of actress-TV host Kim Chiu, is facing 124 counts of qualified theft in connection with the alleged “financial discrepancies” involving over P44 million in…

blocks.text: Lakam Chiu, the older sister of actress-TV host Kim Chiu, is facing 124 counts of qualified theft in connection with the alleged “financial discrepancies” involving over P44 million in corporate funds at their handbag company.

Kim filed a qualified theft complaint against Lakam before the Office of the City Prosecutor of Quezon City in December 2025, citing the “serious financial discrepancies” she discovered within their business operations.
According to a resolution dated Sept. 1, the Quezon City prosecutors found sufficient basis to pursue the charges, with the criminal information formally filed against Lakam on July 15, 2026.

In her statement, Kim said it was in June 2025 when she first noticed unusually large withdrawals and transactions from her and Lakam’s joint business bank accounts which the latter primarily handled. Kim confronted her sister who, the actress said, apologized and admitted that she had supposedly used the money for “gambling” and to pay “personal debts.”
Lakam disputed Kim’s account, saying that she had invested the money in a casino-related business venture but that the venture failed.
The prosecutor identified 124 allegedly unlawful withdrawals from the company’s accounts, which formed the basis for the 124 counts of qualified theft filed against Lakam.

“The evidence on record establishes that respondent Lakambini unlawfully took and appropriated corporate funds in aggregate amount of P44,396,331.65, fully aware that the same did not belong to her,” part of the resolution read. “By exploiting the access and authority entrusted to her, respondent Lakambini was able to divert corporate funds for her personal gain, without the use of violence, intimidation, or force upon things.”
Meanwhile, the prosecutors dismissed a separate qualified theft complaint filed against Kim’s personal accountant, Helena Tayag.

articles.title: Why are European banks moving their gold out of the US?
articles.summary: The Netherlands and France have moved their gold out of US vaults. Part of the reason is fear over US reliability, but equally important is the need to have their gold closer to home in the event of…

image.caption: In an age of geopolitical unrest, more and more countries want to have easy access to their gold reservesImage: CFOTO/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fort Knox, the fortified complex in the state of Kentucky where around half of the US government's gold reserves are held, is a byword for security.
To be "like Fort Knox" means to be extremely secure and well-guarded. Yet the perception of the US as a whole as a secure location to store gold is clearly on the wane.

The decision by the Dutch central bank recently to move some 86 tonnes (95 US tons) of gold from New York to London highlighted growing concerns among some governments over storing strategic assets in the US and whether they could be readily accessed in a crisis.
The De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) cited "geopolitical unrest" and said moving its gold across different jurisdictions would improve its "crisis preparedness".

France also removed all its remaining gold exposure from the New York Federal Reserve between July 2025 and January 2026, although the Bank of France governor François Villeroy de Galhau said at the time it was not politically motivated.

blocks.caption: The Dutch have moved their gold to the Bank of EnglandImage: Peter Nicholls/REUTERS

blocks.text: Several politicians in Germany and Italy — which hold the world's second- and third-largest gold reserves respectively — have called for their countries' gold to be also taken out of the US amid concerns over the Trump administration's unpredictable policymaking and its growing antipathy towards the EU, including threats to annex part of its territory in Greenland.
The gold rush

Sebastien Tillett, an analyst with Oxford Economics, says that for European central banks, outright seizure of their assets is an "extremely remote risk". However, he says there are growing concerns over ease of access in an age of geopolitical uncertainty.
"The more relevant concern is that assets held in another jurisdiction could become temporarily inaccessible in an extreme sanctions, legal or geopolitical scenario," he told DW.

Krishnan Gopau from the World Gold Council says that in general, central banks around the world have been buying more gold since the 2008 global financial crisis and are increasingly focused on where and how they store it. As a result, gold prices have soared to record highs.
A recent survey by the World Gold Council found that central banks have accumulated an average of 1,000 tonnes of gold over the past four years, up from the 500-ton average over the preceding decade.

Gopau says that because the 2008 global financial crisis was followed by the euro sovereign debt crisis and then a variety of political crises, a pandemic, and sustained geopolitical upheaval and conflict, gold has come into sharper focus as a safe haven asset.
"As we've gone through the last two decades, there have been questions and concerns around the global financial system and the state of geopolitics in one form or another," he says.

The decisions by the Dutch and French to move their gold out of the US and back to Europe highlight the new focus on where exactly the gold is held, so that it can be easily and quickly leveraged in the event of a new crisis.

Central banks, governments and sovereign wealth funds hold physical gold in different locations. Moving it can be extremely complex, risky and costly, while the ease of selling it or trading it for currencies or other assets depends on the location.
"Central banks are paying greater attention to where reserves are held as well as what assets they hold, mainly to maximise resilience and flexibility of reserve holdings," says Tillett.

Gopaul says reserve management has become "incredibly important" and that while it might seem obvious to focus on the possible negative risks associated with a certain jurisdiction such as the US, part of the rationale behind such decisions is making sure the gold is as close to home as possible and in a trading hub which moves fast.
He highlights the fact that the Dutch central bank moved its gold to London rather than to the Netherlands because the UK is "one of the most liquid trading hubs in the gold market."

"The idea is that in the event of a crisis, in stress periods, that gold can be potentially mobilized," he says. "London is pretty much the heart of the gold market, and there is so much activity there, and it's such a liquid market, that in a time of crisis that is where you want your gold."
The Bank of England is a major global gold holder and custodian. There are estimated to be around 400,000 gold bars in its possession, worth around $270 billion (€232 billion).
The US question

While moving gold to a location such as London has an attraction of its own for European entities, it is clear that doubts over US reliability in the Trump era and over the US financial system as a whole is driving decision-making.
Last week, the manager of Norway's massive $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund said the fund needs to significantly cut its exposure to US treasuries.
That decision seems to be driven by concern over US government bond markets, with soaring inflation and government debt driving up borrowing costs and spooking investors.
Tillett says gold remains sensitive to decisions by the US federal reserve and that general concern over US financial markets means gold holders are looking to move their assets.

As well as those specific financial market concerns, Trump's rhetoric around Greenland and continued veiled threats towards the EU has added to the reasons for European institutions to want to move their assets around.

blocks.caption: US President Trump's threats against Greenland alarmed EU leadersImage: Federico Parra/Odd Andersen/AFP

blocks.text: Yet the US, and the New York Federal Reserve in Manhattan in particular, remains a key custodian of much European gold, not least from Germany. Although the Bundesbank moved around 300 tonnes of gold back to Germany from the US between 2013 and 2017, it still holds well over 1,000 tonnes in the US.
Last year in a statement it said: "We have no doubt that the New York Fed is a trustworthy and reliable partner for the safekeeping of our gold reserves."

articles.title: Sara Duterte: Voting threshold for impeachment already set in Constitution
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday said the voting threshold for conviction in impeachment has already been set in the Constitution amid the trial against her.

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 1:16pm
Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday said the voting threshold for conviction in impeachment has already been set in the Constitution amid the trial against her.
In an ambush interview, Duterte said there was no need to discuss the issue of the required number of votes.

“'Yung threshold naman, nadesisyunan na 'yun sa unang-una pa lang na susundin ang Konstitusyon,” Duterte said, answering questions from reporters after the Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98 deferred her arraignment.
(The threshold was already decided from the very beginning, that the Constitution will be followed.)
“So ibig sabihin, ngayon na nagbago 'yung usapan, ibig sabihin ay babaguhin nila. Bakit pa ba natin pag-uusapan 'yun kung hindi naman babaguhin, 'di ba?” she added.
(So that means, now the conversation has changed, it means they will change it. Why are we even talking about it if it’s not going to be changed, right?)
Senator Erwin Tulfo earlier questioned how the 16-vote threshold for conviction could be reached if not all senators consistently attend the impeachment proceedings.
Senator JV Ejercito and Senator Raffy Tulfo also said they would prefer for the Supreme Court to resolve the matter.
The Senate impeachment court is set to hold a hearing with amici curiae on September 23 to consult constitutional experts on the threshold requirement.
Erwin Tulfol clarified that he was not seeking to lower the threshold but wanted clarification on the matter.
The Senate impeachment court on Thursday released the names of the legal experts who will weigh in on the ruling on the 16-vote threshold to convict Duterte in her impeachment trial.

In a statement, impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol said that as of 2 p.m., the participation of the following legal luminaries to physically appear before the court on September 16 to present their expert opinions has been “successfully secured:”

items: Retired Supreme Court Chief (SC) Justice Artemio Panganiban

articles.title: Marcos rebrands foreign students committee to market Philippine schools abroad
articles.summary: The Philippines is making a fresh push to attract international students, with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ordering agencies to market local universities abroad and simplify how foreign students…

blocks.text: September 11, 2026 | 1:08pm

University of the Philippines College Admission Test applicants arrive with their parents and guardians at Melchor Hall and other areas of the University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City on Aug. 2, 2026 for the second day of the entrance exams.
The Philippine STAR / Miguel de Guzman

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines is making a fresh push to attract international students, with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ordering agencies to market local universities abroad and simplify how foreign students enter the country.

Executive Order No. 124, signed September 8, creates the "Education Philippines" (EduPhil) program under the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) and tasks it with developing a five-year "international education promotion strategy."

The order gives EduPhil three aims: to promote Philippine universities abroad through research and academic partnerships, speed up the entry of foreign students, including the processing of student visas, and help schools recruit and support them.
The order says the country needs agencies working together on one digital system to compete as a destination for study and research.
The order converts the Inter-Agency Committee on Foreign Students, created under EO 285 in 2000, into the "EduPhil Task Force."

The task force will be chaired by CHED, with the Department of Foreign Affairs serving as vice chair. The other members are the Bureau of Immigration, the Department of Information and Communications Technology, the Department of Tourism, the National Intelligence Coordinating Agency and the Professional Regulation Commission.
What changes
Foreign students looking to enroll in a Philippine university or college currently go through separate agencies at each stage of their application.

The student first needs acceptance from a school. The DFA then authorizes a Philippine embassy or consulate to issue the visa. After arriving, the student must register with the Bureau of Immigration for an alien registration card, and student visa holders must report to immigration every year.

The order directs the task force to build an EduPhil Portal, a single online system where agencies will process documents, school endorsements, clearances, permits and visas, and refer cases to one another.

The task force must also draft a five-year promotion strategy that will make "the EduPhil brand" the government's "official identity" for courting more students to enroll in universities and colleges here.
It must also propose agreements with other countries to recognize each other's degrees and professional credentials.
The order allocates no new funds. CHED and the member agencies will cover initial costs from their current budgets.
Understaffed CHED. EDCOM 2's final report released in January found that CHED only has 398 plantilla positions in its regional offices to oversee 37,443 degree programs.
From 2022, CHED reviewed only 13% of all degree programs scheduled for monitoring, and 84% of those showed deficiencies.

articles.title: JRT Foundation launches Jerry R. Tugade Technology Hub for Bulacan Students
articles.summary: JRT Foundation, the charitable arm of Coolaire Consolidated Inc. (Coolaire), launched the Jerry R. Tugade Technology Hub and donated 20 complete sets of desktop computers to Heritage Homes Integrated…

blocks.text: JRT Foundation, the charitable arm of Coolaire Consolidated Inc. (Coolaire), launched the Jerry R. Tugade Technology Hub and donated 20 complete sets of desktop computers to Heritage Homes Integrated School in Marilao, Bulacan, on August 14, 2026.

Both the technology hub and the foundation, named after former Coolaire president Jerry R. Tugade, are committed to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 4: Quality Education, by advocating for digital literacy and expanding access to technology in Philippine education.

“In the Philippines today, 78% of public schools do not have functional computers, 48% of Filipinos do not have internet access, and only 18% of Filipino children above 10 have used a computer,” said Joel Ryan E. Tugade, Vice Chairman of the JRT Foundation and the President of Coolaire. “It’s important the private sector partner with the government to help with the educational system.”

The initiative also advances other sustainable goals, namely: SDG 10 Reduced Inequalities and SDG 17 Partnerships for the Goals, since the event is supported by the Departments of Education (DepEd) and Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Region III.
Bringing digital access to HHIS

Heritage Homes Integrated School (HHIS), with more than 1,100 students, is the only public high school in Marilao without a computer laboratory. Therefore, DepEd Region III volunteered them as the technology hub’s first beneficiary.

“I learned na gumagraduate ng senior high school (SHS) ang mga students na walang experience sa computer kasi wala silang equipment. Thirty percent of these learners, di na magkokolehiyo. Kaya tuparin natin ang promise ng K-12 na dapat job-ready sila pag-graduate,” explained Dr. Charies N. Dela Peña, Regional Education Program Specialist and Head of Regional Delivery Unit of DepEd Region III.

Before the donation, students relied largely on laptops donated by DepEd years ago. Of the 45 laptops previously provided, only 20 remained functional, according to HHIS school principal Dr. Nica Mae Magisa. With scarce equipment, several students resorted to using their mobile phones for schoolwork instead.
For Grade 12 student Mark Hero Domingo, the new computers will be especially useful.

“Makakatulong po sa amin sa practical research, lalo na sa paghahanap ng RRL. Noon, cellphone lang gamit namin, pero mahirap pa rin kasi mag-edit. Kaya malaki po talagang tulong ang donation,” Domingo said.
The facility will also support teacher development, allowing teachers to improve their digital skills.
“May mga teachers pa rin na hirap sa ating technology. Gagamitin ito ng mga guro natin para i-train ang kanilang digital literacy skills. Kaya walang maiiwan, lahat ay aangat,” Dr. Magisa shared.
Beyond digital literacy

The Jerry R. Tugade Technology Hub is just one of JRT Foundation’s many robust projects for education. Among them are the TIKYO Scholarship Program, which has seen a 200% increase in its scholars all over the country, receiving a total of Php1.5M+ in investments for their education.

Beyond financial assistance, the foundation has also launched its Caring Initiative Series with workshops on mental health, spiritual values formation, and drug abuse prevention and awareness for its youth beneficiaries.

The foundation has likewise collaborated with organizations such as the University of the Philippines Engineering Research and Development Foundation, Inc. (UP ERDFI) to support emerging mechanical engineering scholars, hoping to contribute to the development of professionals in the field.

The variety of these projects reflects the JRT Foundation’s overall advocacy for education: that the effective development of young students must not only include financial assistance but also focus on their holistic development across multiple aspects.

“This partnership with DepEd provides us with an opportunity to make a more impactful and meaningful influence in the lives of students and teachers in advancing their skills. It is our hope that we join hands in building a future where no one is left behind,” emphasized Joel Ryan.
ADVT.
This article is brought to you by JRT Foundation.

articles.title: Speed up electricity grid upgrade or else face higher bills, warns UK watchdog
articles.summary: National Audit Office says failure to implement £70bn modernisation would also hold back economic growth

blocks.text: Consumers will pay higher energy bills unless the UK government speeds up work on a vast programme of upgrades to the electricity grid to enable the switch to renewables, the public spending watchdog has warned.

The National Audit Office (NAO) said that without faster action the extra costs associated with managing the ageing power network, which are ultimately passed on to the public, could reach £7.8bn a year by 2030.

A £70bn programme is under way to modernise Great Britain’s network of pylons, overhead lines and substations so that more power can be carried from wind and solar farms and other clean energy sources to homes.

Labour has said its plan to decarbonise the grid by 2030 will keep consumer bills lower than they would otherwise be, but the NAO said that if the planned upgrades did not happen fast enough then bills could rise instead.
Of the 80 projects it said were needed to meet the target, just 16 are finished and most are in their early stages.
Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said the planned upgrades would “test systems not designed for activity at this pace or scale”.
He added “Value for money now depends on delivery. Failure to implement these necessary grid upgrades will hamper economic growth as well as increase consumer bills.”

When the grid cannot carry enough electricity from where it is generated to where it is needed, the system operator pays windfarms to switch off and gas plants to switch on elsewhere to meet the demand. These so-called constraint costs are added to bills, and reached £1.9bn in 2025-26. Without faster upgrades, the NAO said, they could climb as high as £7.8bn by 2030.

Meanwhile, the £70bn investment will require transmission owners – the private companies that build and manage the network – to more than quadruple their annual spending on upgrades, from £2.5bn in 2025-26 to more than £11bn by 2027-28.

Ofgem, the industry regulator, believes households would be about £30 a year better off if the upgrades happen at the required pace because of the reduced curtailment costs. But the NAO said meeting that schedule would be “very challenging”.
It said some of the projects were already forecast to run beyond 2030, meaning “some new generation” was likely to connect before necessary grid upgrades were completed.
“It is important to minimise this gap, as delays will increase project and constraint costs and postpone the benefit of achieving clean power,” the NAO said.

It added that neither Ofgem, the National Energy System Operator (Neso), which balances the grid, nor the government publishes enough data on the cost and progress of projects, and called for more transparency.
after newsletter promotion

Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the chair of parliament’s spending watchdog, the public accounts committee, said: “Renewables now generate the majority of the UK’s electricity, but the grid has failed to keep pace and is in dire need of upgrading to support the transition to clean energy.
“As one of our most important pieces of infrastructure, the grid must be capable of meeting rising demand whether that is from new homes or datacentres.
“[The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero], Ofgem and Neso must deliver critical projects on time and provide transparent reporting so parliament and the public can hold them to account.”
Ofgem welcomed the recommendations, adding that the planned upgrades would “reduce costly constraints on the system and help shield consumers from volatile international gas prices”.

“Protecting consumers and driving down costs remains our priority,” a spokesperson said. “Funding is released in stages, costs are rigorously scrutinised and companies face financial penalties if they fail to deliver.”

The energy minister Michael Shanks said: “This report is another stark reminder of the cost of years of historic underinvestment in the grid … Our once-in-a-generation reforms are finally building the infrastructure we need: reducing our dependence on the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price spikes and helping lower people’s bills for good.”

Neso also welcomed the NAO findings. A spokesperson said: “We are doing everything within our control to keep balancing costs down while maintaining security of supply and will continue working with government, Ofgem and network companies on the strategic planning needed to support delivery across the system.”

articles.title: Diana’s ‘revenge dress’, worn when Charles revealed infidelity, up for auction
articles.summary:
Christina Stambolian dress from 1994 has defined a whole category of fashion and is expected to fetch up to £220,000

The dress that Diana, Princess of Wales wore one September evening in…

blocks.text: The dress that Diana, Princess of Wales wore one September evening in 1994 would have been memorable for its design alone – black, fitted, off-the-shoulder, skintight and short. However, it has another distinction, of defining a whole category of fashion – what has since become known as “revenge dressing”.
Worn by Diana the same night Charles would reveal his infidelity on TV, the dress was quickly labelled “the revenge dress” by the media. It has its own Wikipedia page, with the same title.

Now, for the first time since 1997, it is up for auction. In December, Sotheby’s will sell the garment, designed by Christina Stambolian, with an estimate of £110,000 to £220,000. This month it will go on display at the auction house in London, before travelling to Hong Kong, Geneva and New York, where it will be sold.

blocks.caption: The Revenge Dress will be up for auction in New York in December. Photograph: Campbell Addy for Sotheby’s

blocks.text: Sotheby’s global head of handbags and fashion, Morgane Halimi, says the dress is in very select company, in that its legacy goes beyond design.

“It occupies a unique place in fashion history because it represents one of those very rare moments when a garment transcends fashion to become part of culture history.” This buzz around the design has been there since the 1990s. When Diana sold the dress herself as part of a charity auction in 1997, it raised £39,098, close to £100,000 in today’s money. The family who bought it has owned it since then.
Although it was worn in the infancy of the internet, the revenge dress chimes with terms familiar online. The dress was a viral moment, and an example of Diana controlling the narrative.

“She created a look that no one had ever seen her present before,” says Halimi. “That allowed her to show her resolve to stand up for herself and reclaim the narrative of a story that would have been heartbreaking for anyone in her situation.”

The dress contrasted with how the public was used to seeing her. She chose it over the more traditional gown by Valentino she had planned to wear. Stambolian later compared it to the black swan Odile in Swan Lake.

blocks.caption: The designer, Christina Stambolian, compared Diana’s choice to wear it to the black swan in Swan Lake. Photograph: Campbell Addy for Sotheby’s

blocks.text: “She chose not to play the scene like Odette, innocent in white,” the designer told Harper’s Bazaar in 2022. “She was clearly angry. She played it like Odile in black. She wore bright red nail enamel, which we had never seen her do before. She was saying: ‘Let’s be wicked tonight.’”

If the Stambolian dress is shorthand for revenge dressing now, Halimi says Diana’s choice actually sits in a tradition. “People have long used clothing to signal confidence, transformation or a new chapter in their lives,” she says. “What Diana did was crystallise that idea in a single image that the world immediately understood. The phrase ‘revenge dressing’ entered the cultural lexicon because of this dress.”

In the nearly 30 years since her death, Diana has remained a fashion reference for younger generations. In 2013, Rihanna gave her seal of approval, telling Glamour: “Every look was right. She was gangsta with her clothes.”

blocks.caption: The dress will be displayed in London, Hong Kong and Geneva before it goes up for sale. Photograph: Campbell Addy for Sotheby’s

blocks.text: There are also copious Instagram accounts dedicated to the princess’s style, including the aptly titled @ladydirevengelooks, which has attracted more than 100,000 followers since it was set up in 2018.

Part of this ability to appeal to younger people was due to Diana being ahead of her time in her fashion choices. “Many of the qualities we admire in contemporary style icons – the ability to communicate identity, confidence and individuality through dress – were qualities Diana embodied decades earlier,” says Halimi.
“Importantly, people are not simply inspired by what she wore; they are inspired by what her fashion choices represented.”

articles.title: Iceland to submit bill that could ban whaling in its waters
articles.summary:
The country is one of just three that still permits commercial whaling, while its government has faced mounting pressure to ban the practice

Iceland will submit a bill in February 2027 which…

blocks.text: Iceland will submit a bill in February 2027 which could permanently ban whaling in its waters, a move that would leave Norway and Japan as the only two countries to permit commercial whaling.

Whaling in Iceland has been put under intense scrutiny since a government-commissioned report was published in 2023 that found harpooned whales took two hours to die. The report led to a temporary suspension of the hunt that year.

The bill, announced on the Icelandic government’s website, follows comments by Iceland’s minister of industries, Hanna Katrín Friðriksson, earlier this year calling for changes in the whaling laws she said were outdated and expressing support for an end to the whale hunt.
Wendy Higgins, of Humane World for Animals (HWA), an animal welfare group, said the bill was a “significant milestone” in efforts to end the practice.

“There is considerable political and public support for this bill to ban commercial whaling, and compelling ethical, veterinary, legal and conservation reasons to hope it succeeds,” said Higgins. “Every whale killed by exploding harpoon in Icelandic waters, is a tragic loss of life needlessly taken for an industry that has no purpose. A law to stop the killing can’t come soon enough.”

So far this year, up to 8 September, 80 fin whales were caught in Icelandic waters, according to HWA. The hunting season runs from June to the end of September and Iceland’s quota is up to 150 animals.

Fin whales are the second-largest animals on Earth, second to blue whales, and are classified as vulnerable to extinction by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, despite decades of recovery after the commercial whaling moratorium in 1986.
Iceland has only one remaining whaling company, Hvalur, run by Kristján Loftsson. A previous interim government in Iceland issued a five-year permit to Hvalur, which runs until 2029.

Higgins said: “Of course, campaigners want an immediate end to the killing of whales, but we also recognise that even if a ban is introduced, it’s likely that the current whaling permits, which expire in 2029, will be allowed to run their course.”

Sharon Livermore, the director of marine conservation at the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) said: “A proposal to update the laws that allow whaling in Icelandic waters would be a groundbreaking step towards modern day marine conservation and animal welfare, especially for a country so reliant on a healthy ocean.”

Just three countries – Iceland, Norway and Japan – have hunted for whales commercially in recent years. Norway resumed commercial whaling in 1993, and Iceland in 2006, despite a moratorium by the International Whaling Commission.
Japan left the IWC in 2019 and resumed commercial whaling in its waters.

“Hindi ko muna masagot iyan dahil wala pa namang papel o dokumento na nagsasabi na kailangan kong mag-appear as witness for the prosecution,” she said.
(I can't answer that right now because there is no paper or document yet that says I have to appear as a witness for the prosecution.)
Earlier, the House prosecution panel said they intend to present Duterte herself in her own impeachment trial.
“All of these pawns and castles and horses and bishops point to only one person and that accountable person is the Vice President," Private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan earlier said.
"In lieu of presenting 15 other witnesses, we will be presenting the Vice President herself for Article 1 of the Articles of Impeachment [on confidential funds],” she added.

“Unless the Vice President herself appears and respects the process of this impeachment court and affirms, confirms her allegation of innocence, Your Honor…the people will never know if the prosecution's case based on witnesses and evidence will point to the Senator judges, Your Honor, exercising the lens of political neutrality, and towards the end, [if] justice will be served,” Kapunan pointed out.

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison, in response, said issuing a subpoena or “testimonial compulsion” to the Vice President before her impeachment trial violates her Constitutional right as provided under Article 3, Section 17 which states that “No person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself No person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.”

“This right is absolute and this is not only a simple right or a statutory right. This is a fundamental right. This is a right emanating from the Constitution itself and one that emanates from the guarantees under Article 3 of our 1987 Constitution,” she added.
Sison also said that Duterte is present in the trial through her counsel.
“If respondent is not interested in this trial, she would not have even sent her lawyers to defend her in this case,” she said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: What Supreme Court's Imelda Marcos acquittal means, and what it doesn't
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has overturned Imelda Marcos' seven-count graft conviction over foundations tied to the Marcos family's Swiss accounts.

blocks.text: September 11, 2026 | 12:53pm

MANILA, Philippines — First family matriarch Imelda Marcos' latest acquittal raises an apparent contradiction: How could a graft conviction involving Swiss foundations collapse when courts have already ruled that hundreds of millions of dollars in Marcos Swiss deposits were ill-gotten?

The public release of the 2026 ruling in September was belated, having been handed down in June this year, but the ruling was clear on the lack of original documents and witnesses presented by the government. It adds to a pile of decades-old cases involving Marcos family members weakened due to evidentiary problems, particularly prosecutors' reliance on photocopied and unauthenticated documents or hearsay.

In 2007, the Regional Trial Court found authentication and hearsay issues in the prosecution's case, deciding to acquit Marcos for violations in overseas foreign-currency accounts and foreign exchange earnings.

In 2012, the Supreme Court similarly considered photocopies submitted by prosecutors as deficient evidence in establishing that Marcos' children—particularly politicians Bongbong Marcos and sister Imee—participated in accumulating ill-gotten wealth. Bongbong is now the president, while Imee is a senator.

In 2023, the high court similarly excluded unauthenticated documents from the pool of evidence in upholding the dismissal of a 2019 civil case on the alleged role of the Tantoco family acting as fronts for Marcoses. Imelda herself was accused of benefiting from duty-free shops' tax payments by diverted to foundations.

But the Swiss money itself has already been the subject of a separate and final ruling. In 2003, the Supreme Court ordered $658.2 million in Swiss deposits, plus interest, forfeited to the Philippine government as ill-gotten wealth. The accounts were held through foreign foundations, including several of the same entities mentioned in Imelda's more recent graft cases.

The court found that the deposits, which originally amounted to about $356 million, were far beyond Ferdinand and Imelda's known income of just $304,372.43 while they ruled over an authoritarian regime in the 1970s to 1980s. The Marcoses failed to show that the money had been lawfully acquired.
That ruling, however, was a civil forfeiture case. The criminal conviction of Imelda, which prosecutors attempted to push forward, was the case the high court decided on in June.
Why did the conviction fall through?
1. Records not properly authenticated

Most recently, the high court reversed the Sandiganbayan's 2018 ruling and acquitted the former first lady of seven violations of Section 3(h) of Republic Act 3019 for failure of the prosecution to prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

Prosecutors failed to properly authenticate vital Swiss records and prove that the foundations qualified as "businesses" covered by the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, the high court said in its ruling on June 10, 2026, but released only on Wednesday, September 9.

"The relevant Swiss documents were not properly authenticated," the Supreme Court said in its decision with Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda as ponente. "The prosecution was not able to present any credible witness who could have attested to the genuineness and due execution of the documents."

Former Solicitor General Francisco Chavez, former Philippine ambassador to Switzerland Luis Ascalon and a Presidential Commission on Good Government records officer could establish how the records came into government custody, the court said, but could not testify from personal knowledge about their contents or execution.
The court consequently treated the documents as inadmissible. It also ruled that their contents amounted to hearsay and lacked probative value even if they were considered admitted into evidence.
2. Foundations not proven to be businesses

The Supreme Court separately found that prosecutors failed to establish another key element of the offense: that the foundations in which Marcos allegedly held financial interests were "businesses" within the meaning of the anti-graft law.
The Sandiganbayan had treated activities such as maintaining bank accounts, transferring funds and earning investment returns as entrepreneurial activities.
But the high court found no evidence that the foundations regularly sold goods or services for profit.
"Just because the subject foundations may not be charitable does not mean that they are already businesses," the high court said.
It added that opening bank accounts, transferring money and earning interest or investment income "do not, by themselves, make an entity a commercial enterprise."

The court also faulted prosecutors for failing to present the applicable foreign laws needed to establish the legal character of the foundations. Several of the entities, including Maler, Trinidad, Rayby and Avertina, were organized under Liechtenstein law.
3. Wrong capacity alleged in four cases
The Supreme Court found an additional due process problem in four of the seven cases.
The Informations for the Maler, Trinidad, Rayby and Palmy foundations charged Marcos based on her position as a member of the Interim Batasang Pambansa.

The Sandiganbayan, however, convicted her based on a constitutional prohibition applicable to Cabinet members, who were barred under the 1973 Constitution from participating in the management of businesses.
The Supreme Court said the distinction mattered because different constitutional restrictions applied to the two positions.
Marcos could not be convicted in a capacity different from the one alleged against her, the court ruled, as doing so would violate her right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation.
2018 conviction reversed

What the Supreme Court reversed was the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division's conviction of Marcos in 2018 on seven graft counts involving Maler Establishment and the Trinidad, Rayby, Palmy, Vibur, Aguamina and Avertina foundations.
She was sentenced to six years and one month to 11 years in prison for each count and perpetually disqualified from holding public office.
The cases were among 10 graft charges filed against Marcos beginning in 1991. The Sandiganbayan acquitted her in the other three cases.

The Supreme Court stressed that its ruling concerns Marcos' criminal liability under the anti-graft law and does not determine whether the assets held through the foundations constitute ill-gotten wealth.
That question, the court said, belongs to separate civil forfeiture proceedings brought by the government.
"Ultimately, when the Court dons its robe, inclinations and personal beliefs are set aside, as they do not have a place in a court of law," the Supreme Court said.
It added that courts must decide cases based only on admissible and relevant evidence. — Camille Diola

articles.title: NSW police settle trespass case after visiting Indigenous children’s home 150 times in 20 months
articles.summary: Trespass case launched by two mothers settled after officers often went to families’ houses between midnight and 4am

blocks.text: Two Indigenous mothers have settled a trespass case against New South Wales police, after officers turned up at one of their homes 150 times in 20 months to conduct bail checks on her sons.
The case, which was launched against NSW police in April 2024, was settled on confidential terms three weeks before it was to go to trial in the supreme court.
One of the complainants, a single mum who uses the pseudonym Megan for privacy, has two sons, who were on bail from the ages of 11 and 13 after being found as passengers in a stolen car.
Police attended her home in regional NSW more than 150 times over 20 months, with many of the visits taking place between midnight and 4am.
NSW legislation allows courts to authorise police to attend a private residence to check that someone is complying with their bail conditions.
But the Justice and Equity Centre, representing Megan in court, argued that many of the bail checks were done without court authorisation, which amounted to trespass.
Megan said the visits often involved police banging on doors, shining torches through the windows and letting themselves in through the back gate in the middle of the night.
She said the visits were scary and stressful for her family and resulted in her kids missing school because of exhaustion.
‘‘My eldest is driving around with his head held high now, knowing police can’t just randomly pull him over,’’ Megan said.
‘‘But I know he’s still shaking in fear about what they could do.
‘‘They’ve already done the damage, and it will take a lot for my boys to start trusting police again.”
The other complainant, a single mum of three who uses the pseudonym Joanne, said police visited her western Sydney home to do bail checks on her son more than 90 times in 18 months.
She said in the space of a few hours, police conducted three such checks.
“The checks often happened on school nights, which meant my youngest daughter was too tired to go to school in the morning,” she said.
NSW police said the officers were acting lawfully when they conducted the bail compliance checks.
A police spokesperson said such checks were an important tool for keeping the public safe and managing risks associated with letting people out of jail during an ongoing court process.

But a report from the state’s Law Enforcement Conduct Commission, released in 2025, found police were stretching their authority and powers by relying on a weak legal principle to conduct bail compliance checks without court authorisation.
The mothers’ solicitor, Kate Sinclair, said it was immensely brave for her clients to bring the case against the force.
‘‘They did it for their families and their communities and we respect their courage,’’ she said.
Megan and her sons have separately taken NSW police to the federal court for racial discrimination, arguing that the boys were targeted because they are Aboriginal.
That case is ongoing.

articles.title: Bongbong recalls lessons from Marcos Sr. on his 109th birth anniversary
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday recalled some of the lessons in life and public service that he learned from his late father, former president Ferdinand Marcos Sr.

blocks.text: Published September 11, 2026 12:48pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday recalled some of the lessons in life and public service that he learned from his late father, former president Ferdinand Marcos Sr.
This, as the President honored the 109th birth anniversary of his father by leading a wreath-laying ceremony at the Marcos Monument in Batac City, Ilocos Norte.

“Of course, I first knew him as my father and the many of the lessons that I remember were the ones he taught me when I was still very young. And it is remarkable because now, I find myself in the position of President,” Bongbong Marcos said.

“Once in a while, I surprise myself when I'm confronted with a situation and have a solution or at least a response, a proper response to those situations. Also, I asked myself, ‘How is it that you knew how to address the challenges that were put before you?’”
He said the way his father imparted lessons was through teaching by example and by leadership.

“He was training me not to become an important public figure, not to reach the heights of political leadership and position, but he taught me about public service. And he always would say that…nothing worthwhile is achieved without great sacrifice,” the President said.
“So, one lesson immediately that I remember was he would ever say---do not ever take the easy way out. Do what is right, no matter how difficult that may be,” he added.
The chief executive also emphasized that the most important lesson he learned from his late father was that “public service must be about your country and your countrymen.”
He said that such principles that guided Marcos Sr. when he was alive, now guides him as the incumbent President.

“Because in every decision that we make, we must exercise judgment, put the national interest first, and ask what will best serve the Filipino people. Because what we do in service of our people is not for ourselves. It is for the country, it is for the people. And you must always remember that there is no sacrifice too great for your people and for your country,” he said.

“It is not a lesson only for those in government. It is something that all of us must carry into our everyday lives. We must serve our fellows. We must do our part to leave the Philippines a better place than when we found it,” he continued.
Prior to the wreath-laying ceremony, the First Family attended a thanksgiving mass at the Immaculate Conception Parish in Batac as part of the commemoration of Marcos Sr.’s birth anniversary.
The President also attended the Natnateng Cook-off at the Imelda Cultural Center, which featured local culinary traditions and dishes made from locally grown produce.
He also witnessed the cultural show “Raniag Ti Amianan” at the Salakot Theatre of the Ilocandia Cultural Center and visited the Mercato ni Nanay Ces at the cultural center grounds. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: The baddest b****** ain’t in L.A., neither is success
articles.summary: “The baddest b****** ain’t in L.A.” Everywhere you go, you might see or hear this particular line—on the radio, social media posts, or even posters around the city. It’s undeniably…

blocks.text: “The baddest b****** ain’t in L.A.”

Everywhere you go, you might see or hear this particular line—on the radio, social media posts, or even posters around the city. It’s undeniably catchy, alright. Kids, teens, and even adults know it by heart.
But have you ever stopped to wonder: Why are the “baddest b******” not in L.A.? What does the line actually mean?

Recently, a song has been making rounds online, with people creating different edits using its catchy tune. ‘Ain’t in L.A.’ is a song by Slovak singer, songwriter, and dancer Adela that challenges the idea that success, beauty, and ambition are exclusive to Los Angeles.
At first, it may seem like a simple message. But behind its nostalgic sound lies a much deeper meaning.
Young dreamer
There is no one better to sing the song than Adela herself.

blocks.caption: via YouTube

blocks.text: Some of you may already recognize her face, while others may find her somewhat familiar. That’s because the singer appeared in the 2023 reality series ‘Dream Academy,’ which eventually led to the formation of the girl group KATSEYE. Despite delivering a strong performance and making her mark on the show, Adela did not make it to the final lineup.
But that did not stop her from pursuing her dreams. She debuted as a solo artist in 2024 with her single ‘Homewrecked’ and signed with Capitol Records in 2025.

However, long before becoming the artist she is today, Adela was a child who dreamed of becoming a singer after watching the American teen sitcom ‘Hannah Montana.’ She also watched American shows to teach herself English, describing her younger self as “Americanized.” Her dream became even more tangible when she moved to Los Angeles in 2022 to pursue a career in music.
Ironically, Adela found massive success after moving to Los Angeles, but her biggest breakthrough came from a hit song rejecting the idea that the city is the only place where dreams can come true.
So, why did she write it?
Challenging the American dream
The answer can be traced back to her family.
In an Instagram post, the pop star shared a photo of her mother inside a room with walls covered in posters of different pop artists.
“[M]y mom shared a bedroom [with] 3 younger siblings and had the walls covered in pop culture,” she wrote.
According to Adela, her grandfather worked in Germany, and her mother would ask him to smuggle posters across the border because Western content was not allowed in communist Czechoslovakia.

As a child, Adela would often stare at a Madonna poster in her grandmother’s room. She eventually realized that she and her mother shared the same fascination with Western culture and the same hope of becoming part of it someday.
“[S]he is me & I am her, but a lot more fortunate and free. The baddest b*tch on earth. <333,” she wrote.

blocks.caption: via YouTube

blocks.text: For generations, America has been portrayed around the world as the ultimate “land of opportunity”—a place where people can achieve success through hard work and where children can supposedly build better lives than their parents.

Adela’s story, however, gives that idea a different perspective. The photo of her mother became the inspiration behind ‘Ain’t in L.A.,’ with the song challenging the assumption that America is the only place where people can achieve their dreams.

“It made me think, ‘There are so many beautiful girls with dreams who will never get their flowers like my mom.’ I wrote this for her and the billion other b*tches who are probably cooler than me,” Adela said.

At its core, however, the song is less a rejection of America than a celebration of global identity and individuality. Adela’s family story shows how Western culture once represented an almost unattainable dream for people living behind the Iron Curtain. Decades later, she is able to look back at that history and redefine what success means, not as something tied to a particular country or city, but as something anyone can achieve wherever they are.
For Adela, where you live, what you do, or how successful you become does not determine your worth. You can shine without having to fit into a particular mold.
As she puts it in the song: “I’d rather be a nobody than to be like everyone.”
Uplift
The song went viral not only because of its addictive tone and catchy melody, but also because of its uplifting message for people who embrace where they came from while pursuing success.

Across social media, fans have created video edits featuring artists and personalities who achieved success without being based in America, often using the caption “The baddest b*tches ain’t in L.A.” alongside their respective countries or hometowns.

Others have connected the song to their own struggles, using it as a reminder of how they managed to stay strong despite difficult circumstances. For many, the song has become an anthem of encouragement, celebrating people for who they are and reminding them that they do not have to conform to society’s idea of what success should look like.

blocks.caption: via TikTok

blocks.text: Ultimately, the song’s message has resonated on a global scale, earning massive reactions and achieving a historic chart milestone as the first song by a Slovak artist to enter the Billboard Hot 100.

articles.title: Elderly pedestrian killed in Brgy. Mabolo motorcycle crash
articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines — A 61-year-old man died after being struck by a motorcycle along MJ Cuenco Avenue in Barangay Mabolo early Friday morning, September 11. Police identified the fatality as…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines — A 61-year-old man died after being struck by a motorcycle along MJ Cuenco Avenue in Barangay Mabolo early Friday morning, September 11.
Police identified the fatality as Romeo Banzon, a resident of Cogon Waze, Carmen, Cebu.
According to an initial report from the Traffic Enforcement Unit of the Cebu City Police Office (TEU-CCPO), the incident occurred at around 5:40 a.m. across Maiqui’s Bread on M. J. Cuenco Avenue.

CCTV footage from the Cebu City Eagle Eye and initial statements indicate that a Yamaha Aerox motorcycle — driven by alias “Jay”, 31, with his wife, alias “Anne, 27, as back rider — was traveling along the inner lane toward Juan Luna Avenue.
Banzon was crossing the avenue from the direction of BPI toward Maiqui’s Bread when he was hit by the oncoming motorcycle as he reached the inner lane.
The impact threw all three individuals onto the pavement.
Banzon, along with the driver and his back rider, suffered physical injuries. The motorcycle also sustained damage.
Emergency responders rushed Banzon to the Cebu City Medical Center (CCMC) for immediate treatment. However, attending physicians pronounced him dead at around 7:10 a.m.
Authorities are now preparing charges of Reckless Imprudence Resulting in Homicide, Physical Injury, and Damage to Property against the motorcycle driver.

articles.title: Hong Kong court jails 2 Tiananmen vigil group leaders for 7 years
articles.summary: Lee and Chow, the former chair and former vice-chair of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, have been in custody since 2021

blocks.text: HONG KONG – A Hong Kong court sentenced two pro-democracy activists to seven years in prison on Friday, September 11, after they were convicted for inciting subversion, with judges highlighting their use of the phrase “end one-party dictatorship” in their political activities.
Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, were part of a group that organized annual vigils marking Beijing’s 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown on pro-democracy protesters.

Public commemorations of the 1989 protests used to be legal and tolerated in Hong Kong and were seen as a symbol of the city’s relative freedoms compared to mainland China. They were effectively outlawed in 2020 when the National Security Law came into force following mass protests the year before.
Lee and Chow, the former chair and former vice-chair of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, have been in custody since 2021.
Lee was sentenced to seven years, while Chow was sentenced to seven years and three months after being convicted last month under the national security law.
They had pleaded not guilty.
Another former chairman of the group and also a former chairman of the city’s largest opposition Democratic Party, Albert Ho, 74, pleaded guilty in January.
He was sentenced to five years and two months in jail.
The Hong Kong Alliance faces a fine of HK$1.5 million ($191,304), the court judgement said.
Lawyers for Lee, Chow and Ho were not immediately available for comment.

Prosecutors had argued the primacy of the Communist Party was enshrined in Article 1 of the Chinese constitution. Defence submissions that the defendants genuinely believed they were acting within the law given Hong Kong’s freedoms of speech were rejected by the judges.

“By severely punishing the activists for conducting ordinary democratic activities, the Hong Kong High Court has violated their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. – Rappler.com
($1 = 7.8409 Hong Kong dollars)

articles.title: JRT Foundation launches Jerry R. Tugade Technology Hub for Bulacan Students
articles.summary: JRT Foundation, the charitable arm of Coolaire Consolidated Inc. (Coolaire), launched the Jerry R. Tugade Technology Hub and donated 20 complete sets of desktop computers to Heritage Homes Integrated…

blocks.text: JRT Foundation, the charitable arm of Coolaire Consolidated Inc. (Coolaire), launched the Jerry R. Tugade Technology Hub and donated 20 complete sets of desktop computers to Heritage Homes Integrated School in Marilao, Bulacan, on August 14, 2026.

Both the technology hub and the foundation, named after former Coolaire president Jerry R. Tugade, are committed to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 4: Quality Education, by advocating for digital literacy and expanding access to technology in Philippine education.

“In the Philippines today, 78% of public schools do not have functional computers, 48% of Filipinos do not have internet access, and only 18% of Filipino children above 10 have used a computer,” said Joel Ryan E. Tugade, Vice Chairman of the JRT Foundation and the President of Coolaire. “It’s important the private sector partner with the government to help with the educational system.”

The initiative also advances other sustainable goals, namely: SDG 10 Reduced Inequalities and SDG 17 Partnerships for the Goals, since the event is supported by the Departments of Education (DepEd) and Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Region III.
Bringing digital access to HHIS

Heritage Homes Integrated School (HHIS), with more than 1,100 students, is the only public high school in Marilao without a computer laboratory. Therefore, DepEd Region III volunteered them as the technology hub’s first beneficiary.

“I learned na gumagraduate ng senior high school (SHS) ang mga students na walang experience sa computer kasi wala silang equipment. Thirty percent of these learners, di na magkokolehiyo. Kaya tuparin natin ang promise ng K-12 na dapat job-ready sila pag-graduate,” explained Dr. Charies N. Dela Peña, Regional Education Program Specialist and Head of Regional Delivery Unit of DepEd Region III.

Before the donation, students relied largely on laptops donated by DepEd years ago. Of the 45 laptops previously provided, only 20 remained functional, according to HHIS school principal Dr. Nica Mae Magisa. With scarce equipment, several students resorted to using their mobile phones for schoolwork instead.
For Grade 12 student Mark Hero Domingo, the new computers will be especially useful.

“Makakatulong po sa amin sa practical research, lalo na sa paghahanap ng RRL. Noon, cellphone lang gamit namin, pero mahirap pa rin kasi mag-edit. Kaya malaki po talagang tulong ang donation,” Domingo said.
The facility will also support teacher development, allowing teachers to improve their digital skills.
“May mga teachers pa rin na hirap sa ating technology. Gagamitin ito ng mga guro natin para i-train ang kanilang digital literacy skills. Kaya walang maiiwan, lahat ay aangat,” Dr. Magisa shared.
Beyond digital literacy

The Jerry R. Tugade Technology Hub is just one of JRT Foundation’s many robust projects for education. Among them are the TIKYO Scholarship Program, which has seen a 200% increase in its scholars all over the country, receiving a total of Php1.5M+ in investments for their education.

Beyond financial assistance, the foundation has also launched its Caring Initiative Series with workshops on mental health, spiritual values formation, and drug abuse prevention and awareness for its youth beneficiaries.

The foundation has likewise collaborated with organizations such as the University of the Philippines Engineering Research and Development Foundation, Inc. (UP ERDFI) to support emerging mechanical engineering scholars, hoping to contribute to the development of professionals in the field.

The variety of these projects reflects the JRT Foundation’s overall advocacy for education: that the effective development of young students must not only include financial assistance but also focus on their holistic development across multiple aspects.

“This partnership with DepEd provides us with an opportunity to make a more impactful and meaningful influence in the lives of students and teachers in advancing their skills. It is our hope that we join hands in building a future where no one is left behind,” emphasized Joel Ryan.
ADVT.
This article is brought to you by JRT Foundation.
