articles.title: Pilot warned Amazon cargo plane going too fast before deadly crash, data shows
articles.summary: One pilot told the other about the aircraft's "excessive speed" but received an uneven response even as alarms sounded.

blocks.text: The flight data released by NTSB included the plane's speed, altitude, and other details like flap deployment as it approached the runway. The update also included the summary of conversation between the two pilots.
The summary noted the pilot's cautions about speed occurred "throughout the remainder of the recording" as did the inconsistent verbal response.
The update said there was an electronic "sink rate sink rate" callout during the final minutes - an automated safety warning about the speed of descent.
There was also an ​electronic "too low terrain" callout, another automated verbal warning that the plane was flying too close to the ground without being properly prepared for landing.

Aviation attorney Pablo Rojas told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that it was difficult to know without the actual recording what the NTSB was referring to when it noted the inconsistent verbal response.
"But, it really confirms that this was, in a way, a doomed approach," he said.

Rojas noted that flap deployment data included in NTSB's update also could be an area of concern. The flaps, located on the back of the wings, are "part of what helps the plane kind of slow down and gently approach a landing", he said.
"The flap deployment here happened much later in the accident sequence," Rojas said. "That's maybe because the pilots were responding to the fact that they were going too fast."
After it overshot the runway, the plane - Amazon Prime Air Flight 7598 - struck equipment on the ground, hit a white Ford van, then continued onward through a perimeter fence.
It then collided with a Toyota Corolla, before coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway.

The five who died were part of a plane-cleaning crew in the van. Miami authorities on Tuesday identified them as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.

articles.title: More than 20 children feared dead in DR Congo school fire
articles.summary: Officials say there was a stampede as they fled a fire that engulfed two schools in the eastern rebel-held city of Bukavu.

blocks.text: At least 24 schoolchildren are feared dead in a stampede as they tried to flee a fire that engulfed two schools in rebel-held Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, a senior official there has said.
Adults are also reported to have died in the fire and there are fears that the death toll could rise further in the densely populated Kadutu commune.
Survivors have been taken to nearby hospitals, and footage of the scene shows children lying on hospital floors in pain.
Some 300 houses have also been destroyed in the fire, the cause of which is unknown.
Pictures circulating on social media show young children lying motionless on the ground.
A witness quoted by Reuters news agency said the fire had been put out by afternoon but smoke was still rising from rubble and corrugated metal.
Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province and one of DR Congo's most crowded hillside cities, was captured by M23 rebels in February last year.
Rebel‑appointed authorities say they are assessing the situation and will release a provisional death toll this evening.
Meanwhile the government in Kinshasa released a statement on X, without specifying numbers of casualties.
"The Ministry of National Education and New Citizenship expressed deep sorrow over the deadly fire," it said.

"With several lives lost and many injured, the toll remains provisional. The minister offered condolences, affirmed solidarity with families, and ordered assessments of affected schools to ensure learning continuity."
The tragedy follows a similar fire in Kinshasa last weekend, where residents died in a stampede at a wedding banquet hall.
In response, the government has ordered strict safety measures and deployed teams nationwide to enforce standards at public gathering places.

articles.title: Germany’s Goethe-Institut is closing in Russia. Russians tell DW how canceled exams are upending their plans
articles.summary: Canceled language exams, disrupted plans to study in Germany and the disappearance of an important cultural link: DW users shared how the closure of Germany's Goethe-Institut in Russia affects their…

image.caption: The Goethe-Institut in Moscow is one of three branches of Germany’s cultural center that'll have to closeImage: Ramil Sitdikov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Germany's Goethe-Institut will close all Russian branches by September 13 amid one of the worst spats in the history of relations between Russia and Germany.

The Russian foreign ministry ordered the closure of the German cultural centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk in response to Berlin's reaction to the attempteddrone attackat Leipzig airport in early August. The German authorities blamed Moscow for organizing the attack and announced sanctions. They include closing the Russian culture and education center in Berlin, known as the Russian House, and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, as well tightening visa restrictions for Russian citizens.

"All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Secretary General of the Goethe-Institut Gitte Zschoch said in a statement. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany."

blocks.caption: The library of the Goethe-Institut's Moscow branch won't be accessible anymore after September 13 eitherImage: Timur Gusarov/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities labeled DW an "undesirable organization" making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense.
'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams

Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates.
Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard.

"I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said.
DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany.
"My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said.
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig

It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online.
Goethe-Institute closures hit teachers hard

The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years.

"This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote.
"I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW.
"It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote.

Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025.
'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions'
Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany.

"We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians."

blocks.caption: Leipzig/Halle airport in Germany was the target of an attempted drone attack in August 2026Image: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

blocks.text: Some DW readers from Russia specifically draw attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions.

"Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries.
Part of the audience considers Moscow's decision expected.

"The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote.
Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship
Some Russians however believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia.
"German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants.

A bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany from 2011 regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so.
President of the Goethe-Institut Gesche Joost called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations."
According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed.

articles.title: NBI tapped to probe woman’s death after plastic surgery
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) was tapped to look into the death of a woman who supposedly died after undergoing plastic surgery procedures performed by a celebrity…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) was tapped to look into the death of a woman who supposedly died after undergoing plastic surgery procedures performed by a celebrity plastic surgeon in San Juan City.

The woman’s son, Ronn Tristan Perez, who is a Filipino-American reality television star based in the United States, arrived at the NBI’s Homicide Division on Thursday to seek the investigation into the death of his mother.
In an interview with reporters, Perez said his mother underwent four cosmetic procedures — such as liposuction, Brazilian butt lift, tummy tuck, and body tite for arms — on March 2.
He said these procedures cost P570,000 and were performed by the celebrity surgeon for seven hours.

“Just a quick Google search of it, those are the most dangerous things that you can perform. So you should do due diligence before you even do it. And then even extra care while you’re doing it. And extra care afterwards. That’s like common knowledge,” Perez said.
“And so I’m hoping that all of that was taken into consideration. That people weren’t just taking her money, preying on her insecurities about her looks and making a quick buck off of her,” he added.
According to Perez, his mother started becoming pale after undergoing the four plastic surgery procedures at the celebrity surgeon’s clinic.
“I FaceTime her, and she’s pale, she’s missing a tooth. I said, ‘What’s happening, Mom?’ Me and my brother were both worried,” Perez said.
“Next thing I know, 3 a.m., a couple of days later, I get a phone call from my uncle and my dad, and it was my mom dead.”
Perez claimed he asked the clinic for his mother’s medical records but did not receive all of the documents he wanted to see.

“I’m not accusing anyone of anything. I need more than that. I need documents, papers, expertise that what was done here is everything that was supposed to be done. No stones left unturned,” said Perez.
The NBI is currently looking into the matter. /das

articles.title: Safer infrastructure, water security sought
articles.summary: A private sector body that advises President Marcos on government policies is pushing for measures that seek to make buildings safer, as well as manage floods and ensure water security, citing the…

blocks.text: September 11, 2026 | 12:00am

With regard to flooding, the council suggested the clearing of the Manggahan Floodway, pursuing the Parañaque Spillway, supporting waste-to-energy facilities and creating a Department of Water Resources to ensure better coordination of flood control, drainage, drought response and water supply.
The Philippine STAR / Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — A private sector body that advises President Marcos on government policies is pushing for measures that seek to make buildings safer, as well as manage floods and ensure water security, citing the need for faster and more coordinated action to mitigate the impact of disasters.
The Private Sector Advisory Council (PSAC) presented its recommendations during its eighth infrastructure sector meeting with President Marcos at Malacañang yesterday.

The meeting tackled concrete measures to strengthen the country’s infrastructure resilience and water security, enforce higher standards for buildings and construction materials and improve disaster preparedness, flood management and water infrastructure, according to the Presidential Communications Office.
“We should not wait for the next earthquake, flood or drought. We need to act before it happens,” Sabin Aboitiz, PSAC lead convenor and president of Aboitiz Equity Ventures, said yesterday.

To ensure the safety of buildings, the council is calling for the full implementation of PNS 49:2026 or stronger standards for earthquake-resistant reinforcing steel and tighter checks on imported cement.
PSAC is also seeking a Building Resilience Seal for homes and buildings inspected and found to be resilient to earthquakes.

Noting that 12,500 metric tons of imported cement were destroyed by the trade department last April for failing key strength and durability tests, the group called for strict enforcement of required testing before such products reach the market.

Meanwhile, Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon said that all major national roads and highways will have street drainage inlets and built-in trash traps to standardize flood-resistant road infrastructure throughout the country, starting with Metro Manila.

Dizon said the policy for a nationwide widening of street drainage inlets and the integration of built-in trash traps came after successful tests along EDSA by the Department of Public Works and Highways. – Rainier Allan Ronda

articles.title: Duterte’s perjury case vs Madriaga junked
articles.summary: The Taguig prosecutor’s office has dismissed the perjury case filed by Vice President Sara Duterte against her former aide, Ramil Madriaga, for “lack of prima facie evidence with…

blocks.text: September 11, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Taguig prosecutor’s office has dismissed the perjury case filed by Vice President Sara Duterte against her former aide, Ramil Madriaga, for “lack of prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction.”

Duterte filed the complaint against Madriaga in March after he accused her of bankrolling her vice-presidential campaign in 2022 with “dark money” from drug lords and the now-banned Philippine offshore gaming operators or POGO.

Madriaga also claimed having personally delivered duffel bags of money to three different locations – the Department of Education, which Duterte headed until 2024; a bar in Quezon City, and the parking grounds of the Office of the Ombudsman – drawn from the Vice President’s P125-million confidential funds.
During the second impeachment hearing against Duterte at the House of Representatives in April, Madriaga claimed that the P125 million was not disposed of in 11 days but just 24 hours.
Duterte in August filed a second perjury complaint against her former aide after the latter supposedly made false statements in his supplemental affidavit last April.

In a 19-page resolution by Taguig Assistant Prosecutor Duke Thaddeus Maog, the prosecutor’s office found that while the evidence presented by the Vice President disputed Madriaga’s account, it fell short of bringing the case to court.

“While the evidence submitted by complainant raises questions regarding the respondent’s version of events, it does not independently establish that the respondent knowingly and deliberately asserted falsehoods under oath upon material matters,” the resolution read.

The prosecutors emphasized that junking the case “does not constitute a judicial or prosecutorial declaration that the respondent’s affidavit is truthful or that the factual allegations contained therein are accurate.”

“The dismissal of the present complaint signifies only that the evidence presently submitted is insufficient to establish the particular offense of perjury under the applicable prosecutorial standard,” the resolution said.
Madriaga’s lawyer Mark Anthony Palad said the dismissal of the complaint was an “important vindication” of his client’s position.

“The strength of a case is not measured by the volume of papers filed, the amount of media attention generated, or the stature and position of the person making the accusation. In the end, allegations must still be tested against the evidence and the law,” Palad said.
Paolo Panelo, Duterte’s new spokesman, said they saw this decision coming despite filing an “airtight” case.
“I warned of this possibility. We understood the realities,” Panelo told “Storycon” on One News, adding that the case had been politicized.
Mans eyed as hostile witness

The House prosecution panel, meanwhile, is considering calling the Vice President’s husband, Manases Carpio, as a hostile witness in the presentation of evidence on the alleged unexplained wealth article in her impeachment case.
Bicol Saro Party-list Rep. Terry Ridon, a member of the House prosecution, said Carpio could be called as a witness if he is named in some bank and financial records.
House prosecutors have alleged that Duterte’s bank transactions totaling P6.77 billion between 2006 and 2025 were inconsistent with her declared assets.
Carpio filed a complaint against several lawmakers and government officials, including Ridon, over the disclosure of financial records involving him and Duterte.

The Quezon City Prosecutor’s Office dismissed the complaint without prejudice to jurisdictional grounds. Carpio’s camp said the dismissal was not a determination based on the merits and that he may refile it before the ombudsman. – Evelyn Macairan, Michael Punongbayan, Emmanuel Tupas, Ghio Ong

articles.title: Israel's Netanyahu to sue newspaper over claim UAE warned him of 7 October attack
articles.summary: The paper said it stood by its reporting, after publishing extracts from a book where the claim appears.

blocks.text: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has told lawyers to begin defamation proceedings against an Israeli newspaper over reports that the leader of the United Arab Emirates warned him that Hamas was planning an operation just days before the 7 October 2023 attacks.
According to book extracts published by Haaretz, UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan had a phone call with Netanyahu that September.
The report said Netanyahu was warned that the then-Hamas chief in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, was planning a major operation.
Netanyahu's office said "no warning was given to the prime minister from the United Arab Emirates before 7 October", calling the report part of a "sinister plot".

Haaretz, which has historically been a vocal critic of the prime minister, has stood by its reporting and rejected Netanyahu's defamation claim, saying its "sole purpose is to silence journalistic criticism".

The report - and Netanyahu's angry denials, accusing Haaretz of lies - comes as the general election campaign in Israel starts to heat up. The polls on 27 October are widely considered a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership.

On 7 October 2023, thousands of Hamas-led gunmen breached the Gaza border fence and attacked nearby Israeli communities, military bases and a large music festival. About 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken back to Gaza as hostages.

Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which at least 73,670 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Ever since 7 October, accusations have been laid against Netanyahu that he did not act quickly enough after the attack began. He has resisted an independent public inquiry into what happened and this latest report will only fuel critics' suspicions.

The report, published on Tuesday, cited three "foreign senior sources" and a Palestinian adviser to Sheikh Mohammed as saying that, in the final days of September 2023, a representative from the UAE embassy went to the Israeli prime minister's office with a special phone to ensure the conversation would remain confidential.

During that call, Haaretz reported, Netanyahu was given an explicit warning by Sheikh Mohammed - that Sinwar had told a former Palestinian official that Hamas was preparing a major operation that he described as an "earthquake".

"Bin Zayed expressed concern that the event in question would not only lead to bloodshed but also destabilise the entire region," Haaretz said, adding that the information contained in its report was a result of extensive research of dozens of sources, documents and correspondence, all carried out for a book, Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment, written by Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval.

"To his surprise however, the prime minister reacted with relative calm," Haaretz reported. "Netanyahu said that, in his assessment, Hamas intended to operate in the West Bank area, and he reassured bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario."

The report went on to recount that the Emirati leader relayed the conversation he had with Netanyahu to the then CIA director William J Burns. It also said Netanyahu failed to brief the heads of Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency and Mossad intelligence agency, as well as the Israeli army's chief of staff about his conversation with the UAE president.

The report was published on the same day that the UK announced sanctions on illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank. The decision angered the Israeli government, which announced several countermeasures, including ordering the closure of the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem.
But while that development made international headlines, it was the Haaretz story that led the news in a country getting ready for elections.

Netanyahu's Likud Party accused Haaretz of "blatant foreign interference in Israel's elections", while the prime minister said on X that the story had "clear political timing, as part of the left's election campaign".

Lawyers for Haaretz responded to Netanyahu's plans to begin legal proceedings, saying they would not be deterred by what they described as the prime minister's attempts to silence journalistic criticism.
The lawyers' letter stated that the report was "the product of an in-depth journalistic investigations and is based on sources pertaining to an issue of paramount public importance".
"In the absence of a full accountability to the public on behalf of your client, the press fulfils its role and exposes step by step the information to the public," it added.

While the UAE has not addressed the conversation specifically, it did not deny it either, issuing a statement emphasising that, since the attack by Hamas, it has worked towards de-escalation, regional stability and preventing violence.

"UAE and Israeli government entities have maintained open and direct lines of communication since the inception of the relationship more than five years ago," the UAE's ministry of foreign affairs said in a statement after the publication of Haaretz's report. "When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities."
Four of Israel's main opposition leaders issued a joint statement demanding an investigation into what happened.
"Netanyahu and his partners in the 7 October government are unfit to continue in office," said Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Lieberman and Yair Golan.
"We will work with the co-ordination and responsibility required to prevent them from leading to another disaster."

articles.title: TV presenter v secret son: the succession dispute engulfing a Ugandan kingdom
articles.summary:
Family of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reveal son’s existence as they reject committee’s choice of cousin as new monarch

A traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in…
articles.byline: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies

blocks.text: A traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in a bitter succession dispute after the family of a king who recently died rejected the selection of a television news anchor as his successor.

King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in the kingdom of Tooro in 1995 at the age of three, died on 27 August in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment.

blocks.caption: King Oyo Nyimba, aged 13, sits between his mother Best Kemigisha and an unidentified adviser during celebrations marking his first decade in power in Fort Portal, Uganda. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: On Wednesday, the royal clan’s succession committee announced it had chosen Oyo’s cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the public broadcaster UBC, as crown prince.

However, at a press conference held later the same day, Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, said that according to her brother’s will, a son whose existence had not been publicly known until his death should succeed him.

blocks.caption: Princess Ruth Komuntale waiting to receive the body of her brother, the late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, at Entebbe International airport last week. Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty Images

blocks.text: The kingdom’s ‌spokesperson shared a section of the document, which says: “I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a son lawfully recognised as my biological son, I appoint him as my heir to the throne of the kingdom of Tooro.”

In a statement on Thursday, Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, denounced a “self-appointed group of clan members” who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier.

blocks.caption: A portrait of the late king on the red carpet at Entebbe International airport. Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty Images

blocks.text: Oyo was unmarried and was not known to have any children. The Tooro kingdom’s prime minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, revealed the existence of a son in a social media post on 27 August when announcing Oyo’s death.
“His majesty leaves behind a prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro kingdom,” he said.

The Tooro king is selected by a succession committee appointed by the royal clan. A committee member told the local NTV station that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership.

blocks.caption: Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki waiting to receive the body of her son at Entebbe International airport. Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty Images

blocks.text: Andrew Mwenda, ⁠a prominent Ugandan journalist and relative of the royal family, wrote on X on Thursday that Oyo’s ​family had not been able to produce a photo ​of the purported son, and declined to disclose ​details about the family of the boy’s mother. He added that, in Tooro, a king’s son could only succeed ​him if he were born to ‌a queen officially married ​to the king.

The prime minister ​called for restraint on Thursday. “There will be time to examine the will, to hear those advancing a different position, and to consider our customs, the applicable law and the proper institutions through which succession should be determined,” he said in a social media post.
“That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our king still awaits burial.”

blocks.caption: Uganda’s president, Yoweri Museveni, lays a wreath on the casket of the king at Entebbe International airport. Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty Images

blocks.text: Edward, a popular TV news presenter, is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of the former king George David Rukidi III.
Oyo, who was crowned after his father’s death, will be buried on Saturday at the Karambi royal tombs in the kingdom’s capital of Fort Portal in western Uganda.

Uganda has several ancient kingdoms that lack formal sovereignty, but whose leaders are revered as symbols of tradition and wield vast social influence. Tooro is one of five that are recognised by the government. Their monarchs have no political authority and are legally barred from engaging in partisan politics.
In 1967 Uganda’s then president, Milton Obote, abolished the kingdoms, saying he wanted to unify the country. They were restored by the current president, Yoweri Museveni, in 1993.

blocks.caption: The casket of the late king arrives at Entebbe International airport. Photograph: Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Tooro are the latest African royal family to become mired in a succession dispute. King Misuzulu Sinqobile kaZwelithini, the reigning king of the Zulu people in South Africa, waited 15 months for his coronation after the death of his father because of a bitter feud involving accusations of forgery and poisoning.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

blocks.text: On Tuesday, the Houthis launched dozens of drones and missiles at southern Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 civilians and causing fires at several oil facilities that led to a temporary halt in operations, according to Saudi authorities.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for dozens of Saudi air strikes on their territory in north-western Yemen in recent days, including one on a prison in the town of Hazm in Jawf province that local officials said killed at least 23 civilians.
A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The Red Sea has become crucial for Saudi Arabia's oil exports since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran, which has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

articles.title: African Parks: When conservation becomes a question of power
articles.summary: African Parks is dedicated to protecting wildlife on the continent across some vast areas. But the organization faces allegations of human rights abuses by rangers. Now, Prince Harry is stepping down…

image.caption: Around 2,800 elephants live in Pendjari in Benin, one of 24 national parks managed by "African Parks" in on the continentImage: Katrin Gänsler/DW

blocks.text: Prince Harry has long been a supporter of African wildlife and nature. When the British royal first became involved with African Parks in 2016, he served as a prominent figure supporting awareness on elephant conservation.
Later, the son of King Charles III became president of the organization before joining its board in 2023.
But reports indicate that in just a few weeks' time, he will step down from his position at African Parks. The NGO claims that the move is merely part of a reshuffling of its board.

But Dutch journalist and author Olivier van Beemen, who has extensively investigated the South Africa-based wildlife conservation group, believes the association between Harry and African Parks has increasingly become a burden — for both sides.

blocks.caption: Prince Harry served as President of African Parks from 2017 to 2023, before joining the Board of Directors.Image: Rwanda Presidency/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Prince harming

Harry's role was to mainly open doors for African Parks, van Beemen says. His fame attracted media attention and helped the NGO gain access to potential donors. But his notorious falling-out with his family increasingly failed to improve the organization's coffers and image.
At the same time, allegations of human rights abuses at African Parks made the prince's association with the organization increasingly problematic.

"I think they now see each other more as a liability," van Beemen told DW, stressing that the full story reaches far beyond a junior member of the royal family simply stepping down from a ribbon-cutting role.
An NGO with state-like powers
According to its own figures, African Parks manages 24 protected areas in 13 African countries, covering more than 20 million hectares. By 2030, the organization aims to manage as many as 30 parks.
Its business model is known as delegated management: African governments hand over the long-term management of protected areas to the group.
The land formally remains state-owned. But the organization takes on wide-ranging responsibilities, including conservation, infrastructure, tourism and anti-poaching operations.

For African governments, this model offers a major advantage: African Parks brings international funding, expertise and personnel to protected areas that many states would otherwise struggle to manage on their own.

In order to achieve its objectives on the ground, African Parks employs a host of armed rangers across the continent, who are allowed to use indelicate methods if and when needed; in some cases, its influence even extends to managing border controls.

"They take over the state's monopoly on the use of force within the park," says van Beemen, adding that some critics of the NGO have gone as far as describing African Parks as a "state within a state."
It is in this context that mounting allegations of human rights abuses have been recorded in recent years, with conservation efforts repeatedly coming into conflict with local communities.
The shadow of the Baka case
The worst allegations of rights abuses relate to Odzala-Kokoua National Park in the Republic of Congo, which emerged in 2023.
Members of the indigenous Baka community reported violence, torture and sexual abuse at the hands of African Parks' rangers.

The NGO subsequently commissioned the London-based firm Omnia Strategy to investigate the allegations, resulting in African Parks acknowledging certain instances of human rights abuses two years later — though the full investigation report was never made public.

According to van Beemen, the report was not even shown to the government of the Republic of Congo, despite African Parks operating there under an agreement with the government. To this day, it remains unclear what exactly happened in Odzala-Kokoua, and how many people were affected.
African Parks has promised reforms, merely highlighting alleged failures in its own systems and processes in the past but has remained intransparent about the entire scandal, says van Beemen.

blocks.caption: Dutch journalist Olivier van Beemen visited numerous wildlife reserves run by African Parks, including the Majete Wildlife Reserve in MalawiImage: privat

blocks.text: Division over findings in Dutch book
The Dutch journalist has meanwhile published a book on the whole affair, titled "Beasts and Men." The volume won several awards in the Netherlands, and has attracted international attention.

But African Parks fundamentally rejects van Beemen's portrayal of the organization, saying his book contains "hundreds of factual inaccuracies" as well as "a similar number of deeply misleading statements."
Regarding the human rights allegations, African Parks says some of the cases described by van Beemen had occurred outside the NGOs control.

At the same time, it stressed in a statement that it has a zero-tolerance policy toward abuse, and that there is training in place on human rights training as well as a detailed complaints mechanisms.

blocks.caption: Armed rangers patrol areas managed by African Parks, including some national bordersImage: DW

blocks.text: But as part of his research, van Beemen also spoke to several former rangers and people affected by conservation operations in several African countries, where he says he repeatedly encountered a fundamental problem perpetuated by African Parks: the loose definition of what constitutes poaching.

According to the accounts he collected, the NGO also treats some locals who hunt animals for their own consumption as poachers, rather than using the terms exclusive to describe professional poachers who kill rhinos or elephants for international criminal networks.

Van Beemen said that during his research in Zambia, former rangers told him about the brutal treatment the people taken into custody on such grounds can face: "This can involve beatings. It can involve very serious torture," he told DW.
Hiding behind a colonial mindset?

The history of African Parks is also controversial. The organization was founded by Dutch businessman Paul Fentener van Vlissingen, who — according to van Beemen — refused to accept the international economic sanctions against the South African apartheid system during the 1980s.

A former close associate of the founde told the Dutch journalist that at the top echolons of the organization, Africans were allegedly considered incapable of protecting their own natural resources because they lacked the money and management skills to do so.

blocks.caption: Anti-poaching initiatives are among the many responsibilities covered by the NGOImage: Mujahid Safodien/AFP

blocks.text: In its early years, African Parks was headquartered in the Netherlands where according to van Beemen, employees would routinely look at maps of Africa and plan where the organization could take over additional parks.
"For me, it was very difficult not to think of the colonialists of earlier centuries looking at the same maps and searching for opportunities for colonial expansion," van Beemen told Dw.
African Parks meanwhile also rejects this characterization, pointing out at the relevant contracts it has signed with African governments.
Conservation and accountability

The scandal also hits closer to Europe not only because of Prince Harry's departure from the NGO but also due to the fact that European and German funding also goes to projects involving African Parks.
The organization stresses that cooperations with local communities is at the heart of its work:
It says that there are people living in 64% of the areas it manages, while legal access to resources is allowed in 90% of the parks. Only four of the 23 parks are fully fenced, it added.
But without sufficient scrutiny and accountability, there is no way of verifying the details behind those claims, as the image of the NGO continues to tank.
Afrimaxx – What Our Heritage Teaches Us

articles.title: Orthodox church sends medieval prince’s remains to Russian troops in Ukraine
articles.summary: Part of Dmitry Donskoy’s right hand sent to ‘spiritually strengthen’ soldiers

blocks.text: The Russian Orthodox church has sent a fragment of a medieval warrior prince’s remains to troops fighting in Ukraine, saying the relic would “spiritually strengthen” soldiers and help them achieve victory.

A reliquary containing part of the right hand of Dmitry Donskoy, the 14th-century prince revered in Russia for his victory over the Mongolian Golden Horde in 1380, has been taken to Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and is now being transported along the frontline.

The Russian Orthodox church said in a statement: “The holy commander is going to where the fate of the fatherland is being decided today, so that he may invisibly take his place in the same battle ranks as our defenders.”

The relic was first brought on Tuesday to the Saur-Mogila war memorial in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region of Ukraine, where senior Orthodox clergy held a prayer service alongside representatives of the Russian military.
The Russian-installed Metropolitan Vladimir of Donetsk and Mariupol said its presence would help soldiers and civilians “mobilise their strength” and secure victory over the enemy.

The relic’s journey is the latest example of the Russian Orthodox church’s rabid embrace of the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine, which Patriarch Kirill, its leader, has repeatedly portrayed in religious terms.

Since Vladimir Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, the church hierarchy has become deeply embedded in the Russian war effort. Priests have been sent to military units and occupied territories; while churches across Russia have been instructed to recite prayers asking God to grant victory.
Donskoy’s relics were first formally uncovered only last month during restoration work at the Cathedral of the Archangel inside the Kremlin, where generations of Russian princes and tsars are buried.
Putin, who has grown increasingly close to the Russian Orthodox church over his more than two decades in power, personally attended the ceremony marking the unearthing.

Critics have accused the church of breaking with religious protocol by opening Donskoy’s centuries-old tomb. The location of the prince’s burial had long been known, but the church had previously made no attempt to exhume his remains after he was canonised in 1988.

Alexander Zanemonets, an Orthodox priest and historian based outside Russia, said the decision to uncover the relics almost four decades after Donskoy’s canonisation appeared driven by the demands of wartime patriotism.

He wrote in a piece for the Carnegie thinktank: “By the fifth year of war, the church leadership in Moscow began to wonder what else it could do to show its support for what Russia terms its ‘special military operation’.”

Zanemonets said the portrayal of Donskoy as a defender of the homeland fitted neatly with the Kremlin’s insistence that Russia was defending itself rather than conducting a war of aggression against its neighbour.
Earlier this year, relics of Alexander Nevsky, another medieval prince and military hero revered by the Russian Orthodox church, were also sent to the front.

articles.title: North Korea spends war windfall on arms, infrastructure
articles.summary: The Ukraine war and Pyongyang's alliance with Moscow have delivered an economic boost to North Korea, allowing the regime to pursue a range of long-desired projects.

image.caption: On Tuesday, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River, with customs posts and warehousing facilities under construction on both sides of the waterwayImage: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un is spending the money that his troops have earned fighting in Ukraine to fund a long wish list of projects that were previously beyond his financial reach.

South Korea's National Intelligence Service estimated in May that Pyongyang received a minimum of $7.7 billion (€6.6 billion) in financial aid and economic value from Russia in the preceding three years for committing men and materiel to Moscow's war against Ukraine — and potentially as much as $14 billion.
That is a significant amount given that the North's GDP for 2024 stood at $26.6 billion.
Kim's support for Russia has been lucrative, and a slew of reports are now identifying where that money is being spent.

A portion of the funds is being put aside for the Regional Development 20x10 Policy, unveiled in January 2024 and which aims to construct modern industrial facilities in 20 regional cities per year for the next 10 years to improve living standards outside Pyongyang.
Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine
Benefiting from Russian money
More civil programs are being designed, observers say, although most appear to be earmarked for the "elites" who reside in Pyongyang.

"Before the alliance with Russia, the general infrastructure was poor due to a mixture of economic mismanagement and sanctions," said Martyn Williams, senior fellow for the Korea program at the Stimson Center in Washington DC.
"With the breakdown in consensus on the United Nations Security Council and renewed trade with China and Russia, things are starting to move along now," he told DW.

"There are several large programs to build factories and hospitals across the country, [Kim] has ordered the development of entire new districts of Pyongyang and there's a rural housing project building tens of thousands of rural homes," he said, along with investment in "the modernization of several sectors of the economy."
There are, however, structural problems that still need to be overcome, he said.

"There is investment going into building, but the large new hospital in central Pyongyang was built some time ago and sat unused for a while, until medicines and equipment could be procured," he said. "North Korea is great at building, but keeping it running is the key — so we look to see if that will happen."
South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North
IAEA warns of new nuclear facility

More of the financial windfall is clearly being put into the military. On Wednesday, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said it had identified a new uranium enrichment facility at the Yongbyon Nuclear Complex with an estimated 28 cascades of centrifuges.
The IAEA estimated that the facility would permit the regime to produce 85 kilograms of weapons-grade highly enriched uranium a year, enough for four nuclear warheads.
Satellite images also show that the North is enlarging and upgrading the west coast port of Nampo and Chongjin, on the east coast of the peninsula, to accommodate a new generation of warships.

On Monday, Kim attended the commissioning ceremony in Wonsan of the 5,000-ton destroyer Kang Kon, with the North Korean leader claiming the vessel was capable of launching nuclear weapons and would be able to "deal a deadly retaliatory blow at the enemies."

The third area of heavy investment has been in major improvements in roads, ports and bridges. This is infrastructure that stagnated during years of isolation under international sanctions but is today required to facilitate the deployment of more troops to Russia and the arrival of advanced military technology, energy and consumer goods in return.

On Tuesday, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge across the Tumen River, with customs posts and warehousing facilities under construction on both sides of the waterway. The bridge underlines the rapidly expanding ties since Kim and President Vladimir Putin announced a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2024.

The route will permit greater truck-borne exchanges, reduce costs and potentially be used for the transit of North Korean men, weapons and ammunition to Russia. It also further reduces the leverage of sanctions on North Korea.
North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine

"A lot of these projects, such as improving trans-border rail and road connections, building customs facilities and so on, were started before the pandemic and have followed an on-again-off-again pattern ever since," said Marcus Noland, executive vice president at the Peterson Institute for International Economics in Washington.

"After difficult times during the pandemic, which was accompanied by border closure, the North Korean economy appears to have grown for the last several years on the back of Ukraine war revenues and cybercrime."
Hinterland 'stagnating'

Noland said he has the impression that Pyongyang is faring relatively well economically, along with a number of cities on the China border thanks to renewed trade, "but the hinterland continues to stagnate."
While the Ukraine conflict and Pyongyang's alliance with Moscow have been an economic boon to North Korea, analysts say, it's not clear what will happen when the war inevitably comes to an end.

"The North Korean regime could be in a difficult spot if peace were to break out in Ukraine," said Noland. "If the war-related revenues were to dry up, the country could experience an economic decline and associated discontent after a period of rising expectations," he stressed.
"I am not saying that it would be enough to destabilize the system, but I do think that a transition to peace in Ukraine could present challenges that would have to be navigated by the regime."

articles.title: France’s Epstein probe identifies ‘potential recruiters’
articles.summary: PARIS, France — A French investigation into alleged human trafficking that enabled US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to commit abuses is pursuing several leads on potential recruiters, a prosecutor…

blocks.text: PARIS, France — A French investigation into alleged human trafficking that enabled US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to commit abuses is pursuing several leads on potential recruiters, a prosecutor said Thursday.
Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau spoke after French modeling scout Daniel Siad, who is accused of helping Epstein traffic women, was found dead at his home in July before he could be questioned.
“We have obtained other names of potential recruiters,” she told France Inter radio.
“For us, the Epstein network is a labyrinthine network. To get out of it, it’s not just a single Ariadne’s thread you have to pull on, it’s dozens and dozens of threads,” she said.
The investigation has so far led authorities to New York and “towards Saint-Tropez, towards Cannes,” she added.

France opened a human trafficking investigation after the US Justice Department in January released the latest cache of files from its investigation into the disgraced financier, who died in prison in 2019 while facing charges of trafficking underage girls for sex.
Beccuau said 26 victims had been identified, including eight who still needed to be questioned because some lived abroad.
“Of these 26 victims, 13 had not previously appeared in any case,” she said.
French authorities have previously looked into other figures in the French modeling industry.

Magistrates previously dropped an investigation into sexual assault and rape allegations against Gerald Marie, the former European head of the Elite modeling agency who is now in his mid-70s, because the alleged abuse was beyond the statute of limitations.
Several women have urged new investigations targeting him since the release of the latest Epstein files.
Marie last month denied any wrongdoing, telling RTL: “I have never raped anyone.”
“I’ve always behaved consistently and properly with women. I love women. I can’t see myself forcing one,” he added.
He said he met Epstein only once.
French police in 2020 also arrested modeling agent Jean-Luc Brunel after allegations that he procured women for the US billionaire. He was found dead in prison in 2022.
The main British-to-American spelling change was modelling → modeling (three instances).

articles.title: Germany sets its sights on Russia's shadow fleet
articles.summary: The German government wants to follow other EU countries and take more decisive action against Russia's shadow fleet, accusing it of helping Moscow evade sanctions and carry out acts of sabotage.

image.caption: Royal Marine Commandos detain sanctioned tanker, the Smyrtos, in the English ChannelImage: LPhot Hutchins/Royal Navy/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: On September 1, when the German government publicly blamed Russia for the failed drone attack on Leipzig Airport, it announced a series of retaliatory measures. Among them was a tougher crackdown on the so-called Russian shadow fleet. The term refers to often aging, poorly maintained and inadequately insured vessels, mostly oil tankers, with opaque ownership structures, which Russia uses in an attempt to circumvent sanctions.

But detaining such vessels is far from straightforward, Julian Pawlak, a maritime security expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, told DW. International maritime law, he noted, is fundamentally designed to protect the freedom of commercial shipping. "The transport of these goods on the high seas is not, in itself, illegal," Pawlak explains. What complicates matters is that parts of this shadow fleet are linked to so-called hybrid activities, including acts of sabotage, espionage, and possibly drone operations and related disruptions."

Germany has not done enough to address the issue so far, argues Sara Nanni, a security policy spokesperson for the Green Party. In a recent interview with DW, she complained: "Russia is financing both its war against Ukraine and its aggressive behavior toward Europe through its shadow fleet." Action must be taken against it, she said. "That is the only thing that could persuade Russia to return to the negotiating table," she argued.
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig

She accuses the German government of failing to take action: "Other countries are doing it in the Baltic Sea, but Germany isn't. I keep hearing the interior minister say that it is technically or legally difficult. But I believe the decision not to do it is a political one. And I think it is wrong."
Finland shows another way to tackle the shadow fleet

By "other countries," she is referring, for example, to Finland. In late 2024, the tanker "Eagle S" damaged the Estlink 2 power cable in the Gulf of Finland by dragging an anchor across the seabed. Finnish border guards subsequently detained the vessel.

Although a court later dismissed charges of aggravated criminal damage, Sönke Marahrens, a security expert at Kiel University, praised the Finnish response in an interview with DW: "They sent a clear message to the other side: We know what you're doing, and we're stopping you. And you could see that after this clear warning, the other side got the message and changed its behavior."

In addition to Finland, the United Kingdom, France and Sweden have also adopted a tougher approach toward suspicious vessels. Within its territorial waters, the Swedish Coast Guard specifically targets tankers and cargo ships suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet for inspection. Vessels are routinely detained if they are found to be carrying forged documents, lack adequate insurance, pose a risk to maritime safety, or violate environmental regulations.
Russia's threats: Just a bluff?

It is easy to assume that the German government's restraint is aimed at avoiding an escalation with Russia. That impression is reinforced by the fact that the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is considered right-wing extremist in parts, won the state election in the small state of Saxony-Anhalt on a platform that, despite the war in Ukraine, advocates closer relations between Germany and Russia. According to opinion polls, concerns about the prospect of war in Europe were also a decisive factor for many voters. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, even described Germany's accusations against Moscow as "the beginning of a real war."

Johannes Peters of the Institute for Security Policy at Kiel University, however, believes such fears are unfounded: "Other European countries have taken a more robust approach, and despite those concerns, and indeed despite Russian rhetoric, very little has actually happened. Russia has not escalated the situation. Instead, it has largely steered clear of confrontation. In particular, we have seen that laden tankers, which are extremely valuable, are now avoiding Swedish waters because Sweden has stepped up efforts to stop and inspect vessels."

After the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said: "The federal government will make those responsible for hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for it." Peters believes: "If you use strong rhetoric, sooner or later you have to back it up with action. The chancellor has put the government under pressure to follow through."
Why did Norway seize a Russian ship for Ukraine?
Armed Russian crews on board

Security expert Pawlak, however, cautions that inspecting suspicious Russian vessels is not without risk: "Of course, any such operation has to take into account the possibility that Russian warships may be escorting these vessels or, as has increasingly been the case, that armed crews with ties to Russian mercenary groups may be on board. Those are risks that must be factored into the equation."

Estonia experienced those risks firsthand in the case of the oil tanker "Jaguar." In May 2025, the vessel's captain ignored instructions from the Estonian authorities while passing through the country's coastal waters. Estonian officials attempted to stop and inspect the suspicious tanker. Russia responded by scrambling a fighter jet, prompting Estonia to stand down and allow the vessel to continue on its way.

"It is important to consider the region in which these activities are taking place," Pawlak says. "In the Baltic Sea, Russia is naturally much closer geographically and therefore has other options at its disposal, including the deployment of military units in support." Farther afield, however, for example in the English Channel between the United Kingdom and France, that becomes more difficult: "Russia cannot escort or protect every shadow fleet vessel."
Explained: How Germany will expand intel powers, and why
Inspections would raise costs for Russia

While maritime security specialist Johannes Peters firmly supports taking action against shadow-fleet vessels where justified, he cautions against harboring illusions. "We are not going to be able to shut down this shadow-fleet system through inspections alone. Rather, the aim is to saddle Russia's shadow fleet with risks and uncertainties and to increase the costs of operating it."

He offers a simple example: "If only one ship a day can make the journey instead of three, that translates into losses of hundreds of millions of euros a day. If a voyage takes not x days but x plus four, that, too, cuts into Russia's earnings. And revenue from oil exports is vital to Russia's war economy."
This article has been translated from German.
What Germany's move to officially blame Russia for the suspected hybrid attack at Leipzig airport means for Germany and NATO was the topic of discussion in DW's weekly Berlin Briefing podcast.

articles.title: Much of Europe already levies a tourist tax – a nice little earner for Italian hotspots
articles.summary:
While England makes its first foray into unfamiliar territory, it’s proved a boon for Italy’s cash-strapped municipalities

A nightly tourist tax may be

blocks.text: A nightly tourist tax may be unfamiliar territory in the UK, but countries in continental Europe have been cashing in on these kinds of levies for decades.
Tourists usually need to pay the tax on the day they check out of a hotel or holiday let, and are often surprised by an extra fee on top of their accommodation costs.
Among the earliest introductions of a tourist tax was in Austria in 1842, specifically targeting those who stayed in spa and wellness retreats.

Similar measures were later implemented in France, Italy, Germany and Switzerland as a way to prevent the inhabitants of towns hosting such high-end resorts from paying for costs incurred by wealthy visitors.
Italy’s tourist tax structure has gone through various changes. During Benito Mussolini’s fascist regime, it was broadened to include any town or city classified as a tourist destination.

The tax was then completely abolished for the World Cup in 1990 as Italy embraced more visitors, only to be brought back in nationally in 2011, with Rome becoming the first city to reintroduce the levy.
Depending on the destination, and sometimes the hotel type, the nightly fee typically ranges from between €1 (£0.86) and €10 per person, although guests of five-star hotels in Milan pay €12.
Venice has also had an entrance fee in place since 2024, although that is only targeted at day-trippers.

The overnight levy is a serious earner for popular Italian destinations. In 2024, Rome made €222.4m, followed by Milan (€109.3m), Florence (€82.9m) and Venice (€38.9m), according to data from Siope, the finance ministry’s tracker of public money flows.

The revenues are supposed to be spent on local services, especially in towns and cities buckling under the pressure of overtourism, or on maintaining monuments. However, the reality is that cash-strapped municipalities use it for other expenses.
after newsletter promotion
“All municipalities want the fee because they need the money,” said Gianluca De Gaetano, manager of the Rome unit for Federalberghi, the hotels’ association.

Tourists mostly just absorb the payment, even if begrudgingly. “They tend to complain when they find that the services in a city are not up to par, especially if they’ve already paid a lot for their accommodation,” said De Gaetano.
