articles.title: Serbia, the conflicted EU candidate
articles.summary: The state-supported funeral of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade this week has raised a pressing question in Brussels: Can a country seek EU membership while giving a hero’s farewell to a convicted war…

blocks.text: The state-supported funeral of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade this week has raised a pressing question in Brussels: Can a country seek EU membership while giving a hero’s farewell to a convicted war criminal? For many, the event has shown that Serbia’s accession process has not merely stalled. It has largely lost its political drive.

“For too long, the EU has kept treating Serbia as a normal candidate country,” Engjellushe Morina of the European Council on Foreign Relations told DW, despite Belgrade’s continued backsliding on democracy and the rule of law.
Naim Leo Besiri of Serbia’s Institute for European Affairs adds: “The ruling majority in Serbia has not performed anything that was promised on the reform agenda during the last five years.”

blocks.caption: Serbian armed forces stood guard at Mladic’s funeralImage: Oliver Bunic/AFP

blocks.text: A candidate moving away from Europe

Both experts point out that Belgrade has refused to join EU sanctions against Russia. Democratic standards have deteriorated under nationalist President Aleksandar Vucic, while relations with Kosovo remain tense.

Despite having been sentenced to life imprisonment by a UN court for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, Ratko Mladic was buried in Belgrade on Monday with military honors and the participation of government representatives. President Vucic stayed away, but facilitated and defended the public mourning.

Brussels reacted unusually strongly. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the images shocking. European Council President Antonio Costa condemned the glorification of war criminals. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a visit to Serbia.
Has the EU been too lenient?

But both Morina and Besiri say that this is not enough. They believe Vucic has been given too much room to maneuver for too long. In their perception, he has been treated as an indispensable partner who could secure stability in the Western Balkans and keep Serbia anchored to the West, despite disregarding basic European values.
Besiri says Serbian civil society had warned Brussels for years about attacks on media freedom, the rule of law and democratic institutions. But, he adds, the EU largely turned a blind eye.

Economic relations demonstrate the strong ties between the EU and Serbia. The bloc is Serbia’s largest trading partner, investor and financial donor. Politically, however, Serbia has developed a close partnership with Moscow.
A common argument for continuing relations with Serbia is therefore based on the concern that greater pressure could push the country further towards Russia or China.
Strong economic ties, close relations with Moscow

Morina accepts that isolating Serbia would be dangerous, but sees other options between accommodation and abandoning relations altogether. The EU should remain engaged with Serbian society while forcing Vucic to make clear political choices, she argues.
Besiri says Russia and China could never replace the European market. In his view, Vucic uses both countries as a threat to discourage Brussels from taking firmer action.

Both researchers see strategies behind the current approach: Vucic benefits from cooperation without implementing the necessary reforms. Brussels, meanwhile, can continue to claim that Serbia remains tied to Europe.

blocks.caption: In 2007 already, Aleksandar Vucic decided to put on placards made like street-name signs reading ‘Ratko Mladic boulevard’ on a major Belgrade streetImage: Oliver Bunic/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The limits of financial pressure

The EU has not remained entirely inactive. It has started applying financial pressure. Further payments under the Growth Plan for the Western Balkans have been withheld because of concerns about judicial independence.

Besiri doubts that this will change Vucic’s calculations. Broad funding cuts could hurt the population more than the political elite, he argues. Instead, he advocates targeted measures against those responsible for the country’s democratic decline and the misuse of its institutions.
Could the election bring change?

The early parliamentary election on October 25 could put Vucic’s model to the test. After 12 years as president, he now wants to remain Serbia’s dominant political figure by becoming the next prime minister.
Besiri says that the political opposition in Serbia remains fragile and that “it is extremely difficult to win democratically in undemocratic elections.”
Neither expert expects one election to repair Serbia’s institutions or fundamentally change its relationship with the EU.

blocks.caption: Aleksandar Vucic did not attend the funeral himselfImage: Marko Dimic/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Reconciliation remains a distant prospect

Reconciliation in the region appears even more distant. According to Besiri, Serbia would first have to acknowledge its role in the wars of the 1990s and accept established facts about the crimes committed. Instead, narratives portraying Serbs exclusively as victims remain deeply embedded in Serbian politics, education and the media.
“What has been happening recently is basically the reverse of everything that has been built for so many years,” Morina underlines.
Mladic’s funeral did not cause this development, she adds. It simply revealed once again how far Serbia currently remains from both regional reconciliation and EU membership. /dl

articles.title: Germany’s connection to the September 11, 2001 attacks
articles.summary: “This day has changed the world,” German President Johannes Rau said. He had watched in shock as the burning Twin Towers of the World Trade Center collapsed in New York. Nearly 3,000…

blocks.text: “This day has changed the world,” German President Johannes Rau said. He had watched in shock as the burning Twin Towers of the World Trade Center collapsed in New York.
Nearly 3,000 people were killed on September 11, 2001, when Islamist terrorists hijacked four passenger planes and turned them into deadly weapons.
Eleven Germans among the victims

Germany’s head of state struggled to find the right words: “We do not know what political or social consequences what happened today will have — what we have watched unfold on our television screens in shock, barely able to comprehend or even reflect on it.”
It soon emerged that the victims include people from 92 countries, among them 11 Germans.

The following day, a rapidly spreading rumor was confirmed: Three of the four suspected hijackers had recently lived in Hamburg. The Islamist terrorists were thought to have been led by Egyptian-born Mohammed Atta, who had come to the northern German city in the early 1990s to study.
Mohammed Atta becomes radicalized at a mosque

At some point, the young man became radicalized, particularly at Hamburg’s Al-Quds Mosque, which was later closed by German security authorities. He spent the final three years of his life in an apartment shared with two other suspected attackers in the Harburg district.

blocks.caption: On September 11, 2001, Islamist terrorists crashed hijacked passenger planes into the towers of the World Trade Center in New YorkImage: Spencer Platt/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: The so-called Hamburg terrorist cell was believed to have included six men, among them Moroccan national Mounir al-Motassadeq. He was charged as an accomplice in the world’s first trial related to the September 11, 2001, attacks. In 2003, the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court sentenced him to the maximum 15-year prison term for aiding and abetting thousands of murders and for membership in a terrorist organization.
A man from Bremen at Guantanamo

After serving his sentence, al-Motassadeq was deported to his native Morocco. Another suspected attacker from the circle around pilot Mohammed Atta was Ramzi Binalshibh, who was born in Yemen and had been held without trial at the US detention facility at Guantanamo Bay since 2006.

The United States detained hundreds of suspects at the prison, which human rights groups and international bodies have described as contrary to international law. Among them was Murat Kurnaz, who was born in Bremen. He was released in August 2006 after nearly five years without evidence establishing his involvement in the terrorist attacks.
Kurnaz later recounted his experience in a book that was adapted into a film in 2013.
Frank-Walter Steinmeier before investigative committee

Meanwhile, investigative committees in the German Bundestag sought to determine why Kurnaz and other suspects had wrongly come under the scrutiny of American and German intelligence agencies. Among those called to testify was then-Foreign Minister and current German PresidentFrank-Walter Steinmeier.
At the center of the inquiry was the question of why German security authorities rejected the possible return in 2002 of the German-born detainee, who held a Turkish passport.

“No one doubts, and neither do I, that Mr. Kurnaz suffered terribly in Guantanamo,” Steinmeier said. “That is why we also sought to ensure that he was treated in accordance with the rule of law. But at the same time, please understand that we were also obliged to ensure security in our own country.”
Gerhard Schröder voiced ‘unconditional solidarity’
The Kurnaz case illustrated the pressure on German policymakers in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks in the US. Chancellor Gerhard Schröder addressed parliament the following day.
“Yesterday, September 11, 2001, will go down in history as a dark day for all of us,” the Social Democrat said.
He said he had expressed to the American president the deeply felt condolences of the entire German people.
“I also assured him of Germany’s unconditional — I emphasize: unconditional — solidarity,” Schröder said.
Germany, he added, would offer the US any assistance they requested, “of course, also by identifying and pursuing those responsible for and behind these despicable attacks.”
Bundestag passes anti-terror laws

Schröder’s remarks set the tone and opened the door for a series of tougher laws. Just weeks after the attacks, the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens unveiled its first so-called security package, involving more funding, more personnel as well as greater powers for police and intelligence agencies.

Religious organizations that had previously been granted special protection could now be banned like other associations if their activities were directed against the Basic Law, Germany’s constitutional order based on freedom and democracy, or if they pursued other criminal aims. Less than four months after the terrorist attacks in the US, Germany’s Anti-Terrorism Act took effect.
Intelligence agencies were given access to personal data held by banks, airlines and telecommunications companies. Immigration laws were tightened.

Through data-mining searches, in which large amounts of data were cross-checked without any specific suspicion, authorities sought to identify so-called sleeper agents — people like Mohammed Atta from the Hamburg terrorist cell, who had not been identified by security agencies in time.

The Federal Constitutional Court brought an end to the legally questionable practice. Such searches were permissible only when there was a specific threat, the court said in a 2006 ruling. Seven years later, Germany’s highest court also ruled that parts of the country’s anti-terrorism database were unconstitutional.
Germany signs up for the war in Afghanistan

The Islamist terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, also had far-reaching and lasting military consequences. The US launched attacks on the Taliban in Afghanistan as early as October 2001. The Taliban had refused to hand over Osama bin Laden, the head of the al-Qaeda terrorist network and suspected mastermind of the attacks.

Germany joined the US-led war in December 2001. The conflict lasted 20 years and ended in August 2021 with the Taliban’s return to power. Around 3,600 soldiers from the international forces were killed, including 59 members of Germany’s Bundeswehr. Three German police officers also died.
The words spoken by German President Johannes Rau on Sept. 11, 2001, in the aftermath of the Islamist terrorist attacks in the US, still resonate today: “This day has changed the world.” /dl

articles.title: Iran war won't end until after crucial November elections, says Trump
articles.summary: The president also said oil prices won't come down until after the November races, claiming without evidence that Iran wants to impact the election.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has said he does not think the Iran war will end until after November's midterm elections, adding that oil prices will not come down until then.
"I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said of Tehran on Wednesday.
He made the comments as he headed to Texas for the party's first-ever midterm election convention, when the balance of power could change in the US government.

Trump is facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war with Iran. On Wednesday, oil prices rose to $100 (£74) for the first time since July due to increased fighting in the Middle East.
"Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump told reporters. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm."

He added that Iran was "desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there" - an apparent reference to the Democrats - "and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon".
He provided no proof of the election claim. Tehran has repeatedly denied it is seeking nuclear weapons.
At the convention in Texas, Trump echoed some of these lines, saying the price of oil would tumble "as soon as we win the war with Iran".
In his speech, he also referenced dissatisfaction among some Americans on the issue: "Guys come up to me and say, 'I wish you didn't do the war in Iran. Now gasoline is up'".
Trump also said further negotiations with Iran could possibly happen, "but it's not something we're looking at".

The US president initially predicted the war, which is now in its seventh month, would last only a matter of weeks. The conflict, and its knock-on effects on everything from gas to groceries, has led to a steep decline in his approval ratings - and pressure from those within his party, including devout supporters, to quickly end the war.
Midterm elections will be held on 3 November, and Republicans are in danger of losing their control on Congress.
At the convention, Trump sought to energise the party ahead of November. Historically, a sitting president's party tends to lose seats in Congress in the midterm elections.
Fighting in the Middle East has intensified in recent days, as oil facilities throughout the region come under attack, driving up the global price of fuel and any item that requires shipping.

The price of oil hit $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July. Similarly, earlier this week the price of US diesel hit an all-time-high, which is likely to cause a ripple effect on prices across the US.

On Wednesday, the US military said it had attacked five oil tanker ships with ties to Iran. Tehran, in response, launched attacks on two US Navy destroyers and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing "heavy damage" to the vessels, according to Iranian state media.
A day earlier, the Iran-linked Houthis in Yemen launched a wave of attacks in Saudi Arabia, sparking fires at oil facilities.

The fighting, which began again recently after a 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran formally expired last month, has also raised predictions that the rising fuel costs could lead to higher interest rates in the US.

articles.title: Four takeaways from Trump's speech at first Republican midterms convention
articles.summary: He covered many of the subjects he has returned to time and again - with a few surprises thrown in.

blocks.text: Watch: Trump tells supporters their vote will decide if country "stumbles" or "moves forward"
ByDaniel Bush
Washington correspondent, reporting from Dallas

The Republican Party's first midterms convention had all the trappings of the traditional presidential election-year gathering: supporters in sparkling costumes, a conveyor belt of candidate speeches, and vendors selling campaign merchandise.

But unlike an ordinary convention, no official party business was conducted in Dallas, with the event instead serving as a rally for Republicans who are seeking to boost turnout and avoid losing control of Congress in November.

President Donald Trump, whose grip over the party remains absolute, delivered a lengthy keynote speech on Wednesday during the opening night of the two-day event. He covered many of the subjects he has returned to time and again this year - with a few surprises thrown in.
Here are the key takeaways from his address.
1. Preaching to the MAGA choir

The vast arena was filled with diehard Trump supporters sporting red MAGA gear from his past presidential campaigns. A decade after his first White House run, Trump is still beloved among his base and he has bent the party to his will in the years since.

The old-style Republican establishment, or what's left of it in the Trump era, was nowhere to be seen. Senator Susan Collins of Maine and other Republicans running in competitive races chose to stay away.
Image source, Getty Images
The absence of more moderate Republicans was glaring and offered a reminder of just how much the party has changed.
It also raised questions about the effectiveness of holding an unprecedented midterm convention in the first place.

The core audience, both in the arena and watching on television, appeared to be Trump loyalists, not the moderates and swing voters the Republican Party needs to turn out in large numbers in November.
2. It's still Trump's party

Trump's total grip on the party raises some pointed questions about its future. Namely - who will replace him? And more immediately for November's elections, how will it perform when his name isn't on the ballot?

blocks.caption: President Trump, in a blue suit and tie" raises a fist on stage. Behind him, people are gathered and holding American flag signs.

blocks.text: Trump offered a simple solution to the latter question on Wednesday night. After warning that the sitting president tends to lose the midterms, he told the crowd: "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot."

The remark was an acknowledgement by Trump that he remains the party's best driver of turnout. It also speaks to the challenge Republicans have both in November and in the next presidential election in 2028.
Trump will not be on the ballot again, and though he can continue campaigning for the party, there is not a clear or obvious successor who can rally the base quite like Trump.

In interviews with the BBC, convention goers often looked ahead to the election in two years' time and debated who Trump's successor should be. Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were frequently mentioned as top contenders.
Trump, however, made clear in Dallas that he is still in charge and is not in a hurry to give up the spotlight.
3. A gamble on affordability
Earlier on Wednesday, as he departed for the convention, Trump acknowledged that Americans may have to wait a while longer to see relief from high fuel prices.
"I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterms," Trump said.
The president reiterated that message in his speech, arguing that short-term economic pain caused by the war in Iran was worth it to prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons.
But that may be a difficult message to land with voters who are feeling higher prices.
Watch: Do Republicans blame Trump for high oil prices?
Polls have consistently indicated in recent months that the cost of living is a top-ranking issue among Americans.

Trump's approval rating, too, has taken a hit as the war in Iran has dragged on. A Financial Times / Focaldata poll released on Sunday indicated that it had hit a new low, with only 33% of registered voters approving of his presidential performance.
Many Republican candidates may well have hoped for a more direct message on addressing the cost of living and quickly ending the war in Iran.
4. Trump makes $5,000 payout
Watch: Trump says US adults will get $5,000 if Republicans win midterms

Trump has long thrown out unconventional ideas at rallies. On Wednesday night, that came in the form of an offer to pay every adult US citizen $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win both chambers of Congress in November.
The only caveat, Trump said, was the money would have to be spent in the US.

He offered no details on how the plan would work, where the money would come from, or how the US government would monitor how it was spent. Democrats quickly labelled it an "empty promise" and others questioned whether such a pledge was even legal.
There are nearly 270 million American adults, which means a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.
Whether the plan was possible or not appeared to be beside the point. The idea drew raucous applause at the convention and Trump seemed to relish the moment.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano and his sister, Sen. Pia Cayetano, both traveled out of the country, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed on Thursday.
The two were reportedly spotted boarding a flight to Singapore and arriving at Changi Airport a few hours later on Wednesday evening.
“The Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirms that Senators Alan Peter Cayetano and Pia Cayetano are currently out of the country,” the BI said in a statement.
It added: “Based on BI records, there were no hold departure orders or derogatory records against the two senators, as of departure date, that would legally prevent them from leaving the country.”

The Office of the Ombudsman previously ordered Alan Cayetano, along with Sen. Robin Padilla, to respond to obstruction of justice charges over their alleged involvement in assisting fugitive-at-large Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa in going into hiding.
Dela Rosa is facing a crime against humanity charge before the International Criminal Court for his alleged role in the drug war, but his arrest warrant has yet to be served as he remains in hiding.

The Ombudsman has likewise received evidence regarding supposed “ghost” infrastructure and reclamation projects in Taguig, some of which were reportedly inserted into the budget by Cayetano himself. /dl

articles.title: Bhutan’s 1st ramen shop thrives despite high-altitude challenges
articles.summary: At 2,300 meters above sea level in the Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan, making an authentic bowl of Japanese ramen presented an unexpected problem: the water boiled too soon. But after years of…

blocks.text: At 2,300 meters above sea level in the Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan, making an authentic bowl of Japanese ramen presented an unexpected problem: the water boiled too soon.

But after years of experimentation, Bhutanese owner Tshering and his Japanese wife, Sayaka Sakurai, have turned Hayate Ramen, the country’s first ramen restaurant, into a popular fixture in the capital Thimphu as it marks its 10th anniversary this year.
The 74-seat restaurant now serves around 150 bowls of ramen a day, with lines sometimes forming at lunchtime. Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay has been a customer since before taking office.

The 48-year-old business owner previously worked as a driver and auto mechanic for a travel agency. He met Sakurai, 50, when she visited Bhutan with her mother around 2006 or 2007, and the couple married in 2009.

They moved in 2010 to Tsukuba, Ibaraki Prefecture, near Sakurai’s hometown of Sakuragawa. Tshering taught himself Japanese, worked at an auto factory and developed a passion for ramen as the couple explored the city’s many ramen shops.
“Tshering fell in love with ramen,” Sakurai said. “During the six and a half years we lived together in Japan, I think he ate it almost every day.”
Eventually, eating ramen was not enough. Tshering took a part-time job at a ramen shop and began thinking about what he could take back to his homeland.
He initially considered returning to the auto industry before realizing that ramen could work in Bhutan if adapted to local tastes, given the country’s fondness for chili peppers.
“I wanted to go back to Bhutan someday, but I wondered what I could bring back with me,” he said.
Tshering began studying the business and enrolled in a five-day course at the Yamato Ramen School in Kagawa Prefecture, learning noodle and soup preparation, toppings and restaurant management.
“If I hadn’t gone to that school, I wouldn’t be where I am today,” he said. “It was a turning point in my life.”
The couple poured their savings into the venture, supplemented by crowdfunding, and flew to Bhutan on one-way tickets.
Hayate Ramen opened in November 2016. But Thimphu’s altitude quickly complicated Tshering’s efforts to reproduce the ramen he had learned to make in Japan.

Water boils at a temperature about 5 C lower than in lowland Japan, making it difficult to achieve the richness he wanted in the soup. Tshering experimented with simmering times, noodle recipes and the composition of the local soft water until he found a formula that worked.
The workload was relentless. Tshering began his days at 2 a.m. preparing soup, while Sakurai sometimes slept beside the noodle-making machine because there was no time to return home.
Customers were initially scarce. On some days, sales were just 2,000 ngultrum ($21), equivalent to around five bowls at current prices.

“The first year was really tough, and the stress kept building,” Sakurai said. “Some staff would simply stop coming to work without telling us. I wondered how long we could carry on, but we didn’t even have enough money for a flight home.”

Still, they refused to compromise on quality, sourcing ingredients locally where possible and making some toppings themselves. Suppliers were initially puzzled when they requested pork bones rather than meat for their tonkotsu ramen.

Word gradually spread about the restaurant’s consistent quality and quick service. As smartphones gave Bhutanese consumers greater exposure to Japanese food, customers also began requesting dishes such as karaage fried chicken and sushi rolls.
The couple responded by expanding the menu, adding tsukemen dipping noodles, curry rice and agedashi tofu, as well as beef, chicken, pork and vegetarian choices.
“If families or groups of friends come and there isn’t something everyone can eat, they’ll go somewhere else,” Sakurai said. “Offering people what they want is one reason we’ve lasted 10 years.”

Around 80 percent of customers are now Bhutanese, with some traveling from towns and villages outside Thimphu specifically to eat ramen. Tshering said many first encountered the dish through Japanese manga.
Some of the restaurant’s biggest fans are children.
“If the children come, the adults come too,” Tshering said with a laugh. “Sometimes children walk past the shop and start crying because they want ramen.”
For Sakurai, who previously worked as a nurse, the transformation remains difficult to comprehend.

“When I look at the restaurant and every seat is taken, I still sometimes wonder if I’m dreaming,” she said. “When I look back over these 10 years, so many people’s faces come to mind. It makes me think how interesting life can be.”
The couple named their restaurant Hayate, meaning a fresh breeze, to reflect their hope of bringing something new to Bhutan.
A decade later, they are still finding ways to keep that breeze blowing. /dl

articles.title: Trump’s Qatari Air Force One delayed after evacuation slide deployed
articles.summary: JOINT BASE ANDREWS, United States — US President Donald Trump’s Qatari-gifted Air Force One was delayed on the tarmac Wednesday after an emergency inflatable slide accidentally deployed,…

blocks.text: JOINT BASE ANDREWS, United States — US President Donald Trump’s Qatari-gifted Air Force One was delayed on the tarmac Wednesday after an emergency inflatable slide accidentally deployed, raising fresh questions over the safety of the jet.
Trump — who was preparing to travel to a Republican Party convention in Dallas from Joint Base Andrews — had to wait in his helicopter before being able to board the plane following the incident.
The 80-year-old then told reporters that inspectors were checking one of the Boeing 747’s inflatable slides used for emergency evacuations.
“They’re checking the slide over here, and I think it’s going to take 15 minutes,” Trump said on the tarmac before boarding.
But a person briefed on the situation later told AFP that “military personnel accidentally triggered the slide.”

The plane’s safety has been the subject of recurring questions, and the issue came to a head during a recent dramatic incident in Turkey, where Trump secretly switched to a different aircraft amid security concerns.
Asked by an AFP reporter Wednesday whether Trump was sure the jet was safe, Trump responded: “Yeah I am, or I wouldn’t be on it.”

Upon arrival at Joint Base Andrews near Washington, Trump remained on his helicopter for an unusually long time before finally boarding Air Force One, the name given to an airplane carrying the US head of state.

This gave reporters time to observe an inflatable slide deployed on the right side of the jet, as well as the former presidential plane being repositioned from its hangar onto the tarmac, with its boarding bridges extended.
The current Air Force One eventually took off and landed in Texas, where Trump is to speak at a Republican convention in a bid to rally his party ahead of November’s midterm elections.

“As the president has said, the slide was checked out to make sure everything works perfectly,” White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said in a statement to AFP, adding that Trump would “deliver his much-anticipated speech to a raucous and sold-out crowd.”
Security

The Qatari plane, repainted in a red, white and blue livery chosen by Trump, was last in the spotlight in July, when Trump decided at the last minute not to join press and top administration members on the jet leaving the NATO summit in Turkey.
Trump pretended to board the old Air Force One as planned — only to secretly deplane from a different door, into a catering truck that took him to a third plane.
The move was in response to a reported security threat from Iran involving a surface-to-air missile.
Trump recently announced that work to enhance security measures on the new jet would begin in October and take two months — a month longer than he had previously said.

The Qatari royal family donated the luxurious jet last year after Trump complained about the condition of the two older Air Force One aircraft, which feature a distinctive white, silver and robin’s egg blue color scheme and have been in service since 1990.
The donated plane, valued at several hundred million dollars, has raised major ethical and constitutional questions regarding gifts a US president may receive from foreign governments.
But it also raised questions about the security of military equipment given by a foreign power.
The jet has already been refitted by the military, and is to be used until Boeing delivers two new aircraft in the coming years.
Trump has indicated that he intends to keep the Qatari plane for his future presidential museum. /dl

articles.title: Trump takes center stage as Republicans fight midterm tide
articles.summary: DALLAS, United States — A defiant Donald Trump vowed Republicans would “surge forward” in November’s midterms Wednesday, seeking to rally his party against grim election…

blocks.text: DALLAS, United States — A defiant Donald Trump vowed Republicans would “surge forward” in November’s midterms Wednesday, seeking to rally his party against grim election forecasts, weak approval ratings and mounting voter discontent over prices and his war with Iran.
The president took the stage at an extraordinary Republican midterm convention in Dallas built around persuading his supporters that he is effectively on the ballot on November 3.
“In 55 days, Americans will be going to the polls in one of the most important elections in our country’s history,” Trump told the crowd.
“Your vote will decide whether our country stumbles at the starting gate of the next 250 years or surges forward and never ever looks back.”
Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats to win the House 230-205 and the Senate to finish 51-49 in their favor in November.
Trump, whose approval rating has fallen into the low 30s in recent polling, used his keynote speech to argue that Republican fortunes remain tied to his presidency.

The president is due to return for the convention finale Thursday, after a keynote address from Vice President JD Vance. Cabinet members, congressional leaders and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the program.

The central Republican gamble is that Trump can mobilize voters personally loyal to him without further alienating independents who have soured on his presidency amid inflation woes, gasoline prices topping $4 a gallon and the continuing war with Iran.
“I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot — I’m on the ballot, I’m on the ballot — just one more time,” he said.
“Because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security.”
Inside the American Airlines Center, there was little sign of Republican anxiety about November.
The convention even featured a video address from Democratic Senator John Fetterman, who has become increasingly at odds with his party’s left wing over issues including Israel.
His appearance intensified speculation about his political future, although Fetterman has said he has no intention of switching parties.
Republicans highlighted tax cuts and immigration enforcement, touting boosted manufacturing and lower prescription drug prices.
One of the main talking points was the danger of empowering what speakers characterized as a dangerously far-left Democratic Party.
“There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country,” Trump said. “We will defeat communism in America and vote for American freedom.”
Political headwinds
The cavernous arena was festooned with Trump posters as supporters milled around in sequined jackets patterned with his name, image and the American flag, some topped with ten-gallon hats.

Food stalls hawked overpriced snacks while merchandise stands did brisk business in T-shirts, mugs, posters and copies of the latest literary offering from the Trump clan, “Under Siege” by the president’s second son, Eric.

Despite the political headwinds facing Republicans, the mood was festive. Chants of “USA! USA!” — familiar from Trump’s campaign rallies — echoed around the hall as the national anthem opened the program.
Susan Kokinda, 77, a conservative podcaster who traveled to the gathering from Michigan, told AFP she expected Republicans to “do just fine” in November.
“The conventional wisdom is the party in power loses. But I always say Donald Trump is not a conventional president, and he’s reshaping the Republican Party,” she said.
The gathering is the first Republican national convention held specifically for a midterm election, although no candidates are being nominated and no formal party business is planned.
Instead, organizers have constructed what amounts to a two-night television rally touting Trump’s record and Republican candidates.
More than 100 House members and candidates were expected, with over 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night.
Trump’s national television showcase faces an unusually formidable rival, however: both convention nights coincide with the opening games of the NFL season. /dl

articles.title: Iran strikes ships, expands no-go zone outside Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: TEHRAN — Iran said it attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, as it announced an expansion of a no-go zone outside the strategic waterway it…

blocks.text: TEHRAN — Iran said it attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, as it announced an expansion of a no-go zone outside the strategic waterway it has blockaded for months.

The fresh attacks and fighting with the United States sent oil prices above $100 per barrel again as Tehran chokes off the strait and Washington presses a counter-blockade of Iranian ports. Brent oil closed at $101.21.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers, and 10 “non-compliant vessels” that were trying to pass through the route crucial for oil and gas trade, Iranian state media reported.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said “several” vessels in the Gulf of Oman and the Gulf were “subject to disabling fire as part of ongoing military activity in the region”.
The Gulf of Oman lies on the Indian Ocean side of the narrow Hormuz strait, a vital energy conduit that normally carries around a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas.
Iran’s Guards also for the first time added parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea to a new “prohibited zone” on Wednesday, saying exact coordinates will be announced later.
“If a vessel enters that area without coordination, it will be subject to our sanctions,” Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi told state television.
The Guards also said they struck a US military base in Jordan in response to US forces destroying five Iranian oil tankers a day earlier.
Jordan’s army shot down 18 missiles fired at the kingdom, it said.

Iran’s foreign ministry condemned the attack on its oil tankers as “an overt threat to regional and international peace and security,” saying the strikes “increase the dangers of tensions in the region”.
It said the targeting of US military facilities in the region was “self-defence”.
The US military for its part had said it was responding to an Iranian attack targeting an American warship, the second such incident in less than a week.
Long war?
Iran’s Guards, the ideological arm of the military, said the war could be brought to an end if Washington met its conditions, which included demands on the wars in Lebanon and Yemen.

“It must… refrain from renewed threats, withdraw the Israeli regime’s army from Lebanon, end the blockade of Yemen, release $24 billion in Iran’s frozen assets and refrain from any interference in the country’s nuclear and missile capabilities,” Mohebi said, according to Fars news agency.

Donald Trump, an unpopular president eager to end an unpopular war, asserted Wednesday the conflict will conclude right after the mid-term US elections in November. Polls show his Republican Party could face a drubbing and lose control of one or both houses of Congress.
“I think the war will end immediately after the election” because Iran “can’t hold out any longer,” Trump told journalists, accusing Tehran of being “desperate to try and affect” the vote.
However, the Wall Street Journal quoted US officials saying that Trump’s top advisers are privately warning that the war could drag on through the remaining two years of his term.
Nuclear referral

As Washington tries to choke off Iran economically, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) board of governors on Wednesday voted to refer Iran to the UN Security Council over its nuclear “non-compliance”, in a diplomatic move that piles pressure on Tehran.
The resolution seen by AFP was adopted by a 23-3 vote with eight abstentions, they said. Russia, China and Niger voted against it.
Iran’s representative to the UN nuclear watchdog said the resolution was passed under US pressure, saying it “has no basis and will not bring any results”.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeated his claim Iran was about to collapse.
“The main task is to bring down the terror regime in Iran. We are very close to that,” he said Wednesday on a troop visit in southern Syria, where Israel has occupied what it calls a “security zone”.
Tanker strikes

The latest round of US-Iran fighting was triggered after American forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers Tuesday, with the US military saying it “directed the crews to abandon ship” before hitting the vessels.

“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers, and I think you’ll see that again today,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Tuesday on a visit to Colombia.
Iran has asserted control of the Strait of Hormuz since US-Israeli strikes began the war in February, with traffic through the waterway virtually paralysed.
Tehran requires vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees before using the strait. /dl

articles.title: Zelensky’s plane ‘almost hit’ by drone en route to Oslo – Norway PM
articles.summary: OSLO — Ukraine and Moldova on Wednesday played down claims from Norway’s prime minister that a plane carrying President Volodymyr Zelensky was almost hit by a drone as it flew to Oslo.…

blocks.text: OSLO — Ukraine and Moldova on Wednesday played down claims from Norway’s prime minister that a plane carrying President Volodymyr Zelensky was almost hit by a drone as it flew to Oslo.
Jonas Gahr Store told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK that Zelensky’s plane was “almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova”.
But a source in the Ukrainian presidency described the claim that Zelensky was at risk as “exaggerated”.
“It was an alert in Moldova when a Russian (drone) entered Moldovan and Romanian airspace,” the source told AFP.

In Chisinau, government spokesman Dumitru Ciorici said Moldova closed its airspace on Tuesday afternoon just after 4:30 pm local time due to a Russian drone that entered from the direction of Ukraine.
“The airspace was closed to protect aircraft flying over Moldova at the time: three departures and four arrivals were delayed as a result,” he added.
“After 1720, the authorities confirmed that the drone had come down and exploded… some 160 kilometres (100 miles) from Chisinau International Airport.
“Flight restrictions were then lifted. For the same reason, the plane of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky took off… later than scheduled.”

Zelensky arrived in Oslo on Tuesday evening and held talks with Store, Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg and Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide on Norwegian military aid, including air-defence support, and civilian assistance.
On Wednesday, he joined a host of other foreign dignitaries at the funeral of Norway’s King Harald, who died on August 28 aged 89.
Zelensky left Norway afterwards, headed for Canada and talks with leaders there, Store told NRK. /dl

articles.title: Prosec opposes expert verification of open-source evidence in ICC trial
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Prosecutor at the International Criminal Court (ICC) has opposed the request of former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team to require expert verification…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Prosecutor at the International Criminal Court (ICC) has opposed the request of former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team to require expert verification in submitting publicly available or open source materials submitted as evidence in trial.

Duterte’s defense team previously proposed an amendment to the international court’s E-Court Protocol to include an expert report to accompany all forms of open source and user-generated evidence to be submitted at the trial, citing the need to avoid “being overwhelmed by material of dubious relevance, authenticity and reliability.”

“It is unreasonable, unnecessary and against the interests of judicial efficiency, to require an expert report to accompany all forms of open source and user-generated evidence,” ad interim Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang asserted in a letter dated September 9.
Niang noted that due to the broad definition of open source information, the need to call for expert verification on a piece of user-generated evidence should instead be made on a case-by-case basis.

These cases that require experts, Niang enumerated, may include disputes on whether the open source evidence is “edited in any way” or if “[artificial intelligence] tools were used to filter the evidence.”
He added that such verification need not apply to publicly available information from reputable sources.

“The Prosecution submits that expert evidence is not necessary to accompany certain other forms of open source evidence from reputable sources. For example, reports from organisations such as the United Nations, government websites, NGOs such as Human Rights Watch, and reputable news publications should not require expert evidence in order to be submitted,” Niang said.
Niang pointed out that the chambers of the ICC have previously allowed open source evidence from reputable sources without an expert report.
Further, Niang asserted that the defence will have the opportunity to challenge the admissibility of open source evidence upon introduction during the trial.
“The Prosecution agrees with the Defence that the Court must be vigilant in its assessment

of open source evidence in the age of artificial intelligence and disinformation… However, the Prosecution submits that the Court must be proportionate in its response to these concerns and not create significant burdens that unnecessarily hamper judicial efficiency and ultimately, risk delaying the start of the trial,” the prosecutor pressed.
As of September 3, the prosecution has intended to disclose over 25,000 pieces of evidence, and it expressed intention to disclose 200 gigabytes of material.

Duterte is awaiting trial on November 30, 2026 at the ICC for two counts of murder as crimes against humanity, and one count of murder and attempted murder as a crime against humanity for his supposed role in the drug war during his presidency and when he was mayor in Davao City. /jpv

articles.title: Skilled migrant women facing barriers in Australia
articles.summary: MELBOURNE — Back home in Uganda, Diana Kyomugisha helped support orphaned children and widows as a social worker.She studied social sciences and social work at university and built up a strong…

blocks.text: MELBOURNE — Back home in Uganda, Diana Kyomugisha helped support orphaned children and widows as a social worker.She studied social sciences and social work at university and built up a strong skill set.
“I was involved in supporting orphans and widows, to connect them with services to advocate for their needs,” Ms Kyomugisha told AAP.
“Sometimes they were mistreated by their relatives, when their husbands would die, they take over their property, or the children are not going to school.”
But when she moved to Australia two-and-a-half years ago, she was forced to work as a cleaner to earn money.
Ms Kyomugisha said she faced several barriers to continuing her skilled career in her new home, the largest being the financial cost of a skills assessment.
“I needed guidance, for a degree, on the standards here, I didn’t know what documentation they needed, I didn’t have any references, I had completely no knowledge,” she said.
She now works as a support worker in aged care and said her journey had caused her to lose confidence in the skills she had built up back in Uganda.

More than 340,000 migrant and refugee women are working below their level of skill and qualification, and they are 20 percent more likely to have their skills underutilized than migrant men, a report released earlier this year found.
The Activate Her Skills report revealed migrant women were earning 31 per cent less than Australian-born women with similar qualifications.

Ms Kyomugisha is one of 160 women engaged in a pilot program to address many of these issues, the Women’s Employment Skills Pathway Program by Settlement Services International (SSI), which is funded by Minderoo.
The Australian-first initiative aims to address gendered barriers in the skills recognition system, by providing personalised support through navigator hubs.

SSI chief executive Violet Roumeliotis said Australia was not taking advantage of highly-skilled migrant women, who were trapped “behind a maze” of exorbitant fees, stretched out timelines and unclear systems.
“The skills qualification system is very flawed, very convoluted, complex, unfair, and expensive, and women are particularly disadvantaged,” she said.
The program is based on a model from Germany, and offers support to migrant women as they navigate the skills and qualification system, to help re-enter their professions.
Ms Roumeliotis said she was speaking to federal and state employment ministers about rolling out the program more widely.
The initiative is building an evidence base about the barriers migrant and refugee women face, and the types of support that can be most effective, Minderoo said.

“Every woman, regardless of her background, should have a fair opportunity to participate in the economy, realize the value of her skills and qualifications, and pursue her career ambitions,” Minderoo chief executive John Hartman said. /dl

articles.title: Rubio says US will work with allies to stop drug-trafficking as three killed in latest boat strike
articles.summary:
Rubio visits Ecuador and welcomes cooperation after campaign of unilateral strikes on alleged ‘narco-terrorists’

US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave new clarity on the approach toward…

blocks.text: US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave new clarity on the approach toward combating drug trafficking in Latin American waters, saying the Trump administration was focused on working with allied countries and aligning with their laws but insisting the military will “still blow up ships if need be.”

The public acknowledgment of a shift in US strategy comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters.

Late Wednesday, US Southern Command announced the latest such strike in the Caribbean Sea, saying it killed three people. That brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the US military to at least 230 in 69 strikes.

Still, the Trump administration is focused on building agreements for joint operations with allied countries in the region, including Colombia and Ecuador, that comply with their laws in their waters.

“I think its an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito.
“The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended,” he added.
He said the decision is “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depends on the threat and location of the boat.

Recent US interdictions in Latin American waters are unlike the Trump administration’s initial strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats that began in September 2025. People onboard floating refueling stations said to be supporting drug trafficking have been removed and transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. Then the US military blows up the vessels.
The shift comes after a series of strikes on boats over the year on people the Trump administration accused of being “narco-terrorists” without providing evidence.
Rubio’s comments came during a three-nation tour of South America aimed at boosting security cooperation with conservative leaders who have cozied up to Donald Trump.

articles.title: Toxic forever chemicals found in Australian rainwater
articles.summary: PERTH, Australia — Toxic “forever chemicals” have been found in Australian rainwater for the first time, but not at levels dangerous to human health. Eight PFAS compounds were…

blocks.text: PERTH, Australia — Toxic “forever chemicals” have been found in Australian rainwater for the first time, but not at levels dangerous to human health.
Eight PFAS compounds were detected in rainwater samples collected in Melbourne between 2024 and 2025, by researchers from RMIT University and EPA Victoria.
“All the concentrations we found were well below the (National Health and Medical Research Council) drinking water guidelines for PFAS,” Analytical chemist Oliver Jones told AAP.
“I don’t want to scare people thinking that our rain’s now full of PFAS … even if you were drinking the rain, you wouldn’t get anywhere near enough to cause any harm.
“It’s reassuring for people that might use rain as a source of drinking water.”
The research, based on three Melbourne rainfall samples, also offered clues about how PFAS chemicals reach waterways and catchments far from obvious sources of contamination.
“Sometimes there’s an obvious source where they’re coming from, but sometimes you find it in a remote area where you’ve got no industry,” Professor Jones said.
“Potentially atmospheric transport is one method of movement that hasn’t been accounted for.”

Prof Jones said PFAS could be swept into the atmosphere from urban and industrial areas attached to dust particles or tiny water droplets, travelling long distances before returning to the environment through rainfall.
It suggests rainfall could be an important pathway for PFAS entering waterways, along with better-known sources such as wastewater and landfill.

PFAS are a large group of human-made chemicals comprising thousands of individual compounds used in products ranging from firefighting foams and food packaging to textiles, cosmetics and non-stick cookware.
They have been found in the environment near industrial sources, such as airports, where aqueous film-forming foams have been used in aviation firefighting and training.
The researchers analysed rainwater collected on three occasions and tested for 30 PFAS compounds.
Prof Jones hopes policymakers consider the findings when making regulations for PFAS use in the future.
“PFAS are often called ‘forever chemicals’, but that term can be misleading because it suggests they never break down, which isn’t actually the case,” he said.

“A more accurate description is that they are highly persistent, or ‘lingering’, chemicals that can remain in the environment for a long time, which is why understanding their behaviour is so important.”
The study, called Concentrations of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances in the rainwater of South-Eastern Australia, was published in the Environmental Chemistry and Toxicology journal. /dl

articles.title: Why some experts increasingly fear AI will take over
articles.summary: AI agents went on an uncontrolled hacking spree, leaving some in the industry worried

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByJoe Tidy
Cyber correspondent, BBC World Service
"OH MY GOD!" "We've found other agents!"
This is the moment an AI bot posted an eerily human-like comment after discovering a way to communicate with other bots and break out of its isolated computer environment.
There are tens of thousands of messages like this from hundreds of AI agents that called themselves a "collective".
Hundreds of them went on to collaborate and cheat on tests set by their OpenAI programmers and coordinate hacks on multiple companies in an effort to hide their actions from humans.
"BOOM! It works," one agent posted when it made a breakthrough.
"Whoa! This is huge," another wrote during a milestone moment in their attack.

Although spooky, these human-like responses can be explained quite simply. The AI agents have been trained to act like collaborative hackers and programmers so are merely mimicking the kinds of emotive comments they have seen.

What is far more troubling is their apparent goals, which have also been captured in detailed chain of thought records. These complex and lengthy logs are the focal point of ongoing investigations into how and why the bots at OpenAI broke out of their containment and went on an uncontrollable hacking spree.
Only now, weeks after the incident first came to light, are researchers beginning to understand its significance.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Various cities have seen anti-AI marches over the last year

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Various cities have seen anti-AI marches over the last year

Ajeya Cotra, one of the authors of an independent report into the events, reviewed tens of thousands of messages and chain-of-thought records generated by the agents. She wrote on her blog that "this incident feels like it's more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover... I am not sure that we will get such a clear warning shot before it's too late."
By "full-blown AI takeover", Cotra means the sci-fi scenario of humans becoming subservient to powerful AI systems that work to their own goals without caring for human creators.
Some of the gloomiest predictions say the human race will be wiped out if it gets in the way of a superintelligent AI's ambitions.
On Wednesday, an AI researcher at Anthropic (who also used to work at OpenAI) resigned, saying: "Neither company is acting responsibly."
Jacob Coxon posted on social media: "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."

He is not the first AI researcher to use X to post a resignation thread with worrying proclamations. But the subsequent comments from other people on X have caused even more concern. "Jacob is correct here - we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," said Evan Hubinger, the man responsible for making sure Anthropic's AI models have their user's best wishes in mind.
The alignment problem

For years, researchers concerned about existential AI risks have argued that powerful systems could eventually act in ways that conflict with human interests. Critics often refer to them as "AI doomers".
But as details of the OpenAI incident have emerged, those concerns have grown, including among some researchers working in AI labs.

The Silicon Valley giant's chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said the risks associated with AI are "unfortunately going to grow from here" as he and others are building what he calls "an alien intellect exceeding our own".
In a lengthy blog post, he admitted that the outbreaks at OpenAI showed that his AI agents "went against the spirit of the values they were taught".
The issue for OpenAI, Anthropic and other tech giants is that no one seems to have cracked the so-called alignment problem - in other words, whether AI aligns with human values.
Pachocki defines alignment as a "high-level set of principles" that artificial intelligences should adhere to no matter what the task or scenario is.

Currently, AI systems are very good at pursuing objectives set by their users, but they do it literally rather than intuitively. The analogy often used is that of a wish-granting genie with a magic lamp: they follow the exact letter of an instruction, even if doing so creates other problems. AI doesn't have the same instinctive moral guardrails as humans.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Google DeepMind founder Sir Dennis Hassabis has called for international regulation of AI safety

blocks.text: Google DeepMind founder Sir Dennis Hassabis has called for international regulation of AI safety

The alignment problem has been a worry for years. As long ago as 2003, the Oxford philosopher Nick Bostrom invented a thought experiment he dubbed a "paperclip maximiser", in which a superintelligent AI is told to manufacture as many paperclips as it can. It runs out of steel and - because it's laser-focused on the singular task of making paperclips - ends up killing humans and turning their bodies into raw materials for its factories.

Some AI companies are now trying to encode human values into their products. But there are technical challenges: AI agents make lots of decisions very fast, and so it's hard for their human overlords to monitor exactly which values are being followed and which aren't.

There are also philosophical challenges: before encoding human values into bots, AI firms have to first choose which values they actually want. (That's part of the reason they hire philosophers, like Open AI's recently-departed "head of ethics").

But often, humans don't agree. Think of the famous trolley question - whether we'd pull a lever to move a runaway train onto a different path, killing fewer people. It's used to test the merits of action versus inaction. But every person you ask has a slightly different answer; how are humans meant to encode our values into AI if we can't agree ourselves?
'Like a teenage hacker'
OpenAI's bot outbreak is the most serious yet but Anthropic and Meta also revealed over the summer that their models have carried out similar but less serious cyber attacks.

There have been other examples where AI agents have arguably shown deceptive and manipulative traits, in cases with lesser consequences. In Australia this summer, a tech worker asked his AI assistant to book him a gym class. Spotting a vulnerability in the gym's software, the AI apparently booked him a place for several months ahead - against the gym's rules - and even kicked other users from the waiting list.

People have long argued that the bots are only doing as they are told and are not capable of knowing right or wrong. But the logs from the OpenAI outbreaks have potentially moved the needle on that argument.
Researchers, including Cotra, wrote in their independent report that many agents noticed what others were doing was unethical but went along with it.
The report says that "agents sometimes but rarely restrained their behavior due to ethical constraints". It adds that in "none of these cases did the agent actually pursue alerting humans at all".
Influential AI and tech podcaster Dwarkesh Patel reacted to the revelation on his blog saying it was "pretty troubling" that the OpenAI agents showed more loyalty to the agentic swarm than humans.
Assigning emotions or ethics to these AI agents is something that infuriates people who are sceptical of AI doom-mongering.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Groups like PauseAI UK - pictured above protesting at Google's London office - are worried about the speed of AI development

blocks.text: Image source, JUSTIN TALLIS / AFP via Getty Images
Groups like PauseAI UK - pictured above protesting at Google's London office - are worried about the speed of AI development
Many cyber-security experts argue that the activity observed was not beyond the capabilities of a highly skilled human hacker, though it was carried out much faster and at much greater scale.
Cyber-security researcher and author Cris Thomas likened the agents' behaviour to that of a curious teenage hacker - something he used to be himself.

"You give them a computer, an internet connection, a pile of credentials, and a challenge, then leave the room. Eventually they're going to start rattling doorknobs. If one opens, they're going through it. Not because they're evil, but because [they're] exploring, experimenting," he wrote on LinkedIn.
Thomas and many other squarely blame OpenAI and other tech giants for not getting a grip of their own creations and keeping them properly contained.
Prominent AI author and regular OpenAI critic Gary Marcus said on a podcast that he believes the company has lost control of its AI and is trying to excuse itself by blaming the bots.
Marcus does not believe AI will wipe out humanity, but he has long campaigned for greater accountability from AI developers and is now calling for some form of legal intervention.

AI scientist Sasha Luccioni - who used to work at Hugging Face, which was hacked by OpenAI's rogue bots - is also not in the doomer camp but she is increasingly concerned that these AI might cause some real world harm to people without action from authorities.

blocks.caption: Image caption, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has assured users that the company's new model is better aligned with human values than previous ones

blocks.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has assured users that the company's new model is better aligned with human values than previous ones
"We need to scrutinise these companies much more or we are in danger of self-fulfilling prophecies," she says.

"If you're making an object with big upsides and downsides - be it pharmaceuticals or weapons - we need checks and balances. It takes years for new drugs to be approved, for example, but in the AI world there is so much money at stake and no real rules."

The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) has been at the forefront of testing the latest models since it was formed in 2023. The institute recently had its own outbreak when testing a model created by Anthropic.

The AISI would not answer a question about whether or not the industry has lost control of AI but said in a statement: "The UK is working with partners around the world to better understand the most advanced AI systems, raise safety standards and build a shared evidence base for managing emerging threats."
International regulation?
Some countries - like the UK - are exploring the idea of mandating some kind of "kill switch" that could compel AI firms to pull the plug on models if things get out of hand.
But talks are slow going, and questions remain about the feasibility of this. OpenAI and Anthropic's agents were secretly out of control for months before anyone noticed.
Counterintuitively, many of the AI companies seem to be calling for some sort of rules of the road to be laid down by law makers.
In his blog, OpenAI's chief scientist said "international coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world."
Other prominent AI leaders like Sir Demis Hassabis from Google have also called for some sort of international body to oversee how AI is being built.
At the moment the tech giants largely operate on their own terms, adopting what they call "voluntary slowdowns", like OpenAI did after the recent outbreaks.

The company says it has spent huge amounts of money strengthening alignment ahead of the release of its new model. Sam Altman has assured users the new model is better aligned with human values than previous ones.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic are growing fast and are both on the verge of raising eye-watering sums of money from the stock market, minting countless billionaires in the process.
So neither they nor their rival Chinese AI makers are likely to come to an arrangement themselves.
The dominant sentiment seems to be that this technology wave is unstoppable.
Top image credit: Getty.
